Guard me from the emptiness of chasing a number that never arrives. <break time="1.1s" /> I will define what is enough and let the rest become generosity. <break time="1.1s" /> Go content with daily bread, free from the tyranny of always needing more. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-m-debt: On Carrying the Weight of Debt. <break time="1.8s" /> The debt is heavy, and pretending it isn’t only makes it heavier. Lay it down here for a moment. <break time="1.1s" /> “The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 22, verse 7. <break time="1.1s" /> Scripture is blunt: the borrower is slave to the lender. If you carry business debt, a credit line stretched thin, or founders who put personal cards on the line, you know that servitude in your gut. It shapes decisions, steals sleep, and whispers that you’ll never be free. But Proverbs describes debt honestly without condemning you for it. Many good businesses use borrowed capital; the danger is when debt owns your peace and dictates your choices out of panic. God is not ashamed of you for the position you’re in. He is inviting you to face it in the light rather than the dark. Build the boring, faithful plan: know the real number, name the interest, order the payoffs, and stop adding to it where you can. Resist the shortcut that promises to erase it overnight, because that shortcut usually deepens the hole. Freedom from debt is rarely a miracle moment; it’s a hundred disciplined months. And through all of them, remember your worth was never the balance you owe. You are held by a God who canceled the one debt you could never repay. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, this weight is real and I’m tired of carrying it alone. Give me courage to face the numbers honestly and patience for the long climb out. Free my peace from what I owe, even before the balance reaches zero. <break time="1.1s" /> I will face my debt in the light and walk the slow road to freedom. <break time="1.1s" /> Go steadily, unashamed and unhurried, held by the One who canceled your greatest debt. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-m-tool: On Money as Tool, Not Master. <break time="1.8s" /> Take stock of who is actually serving whom in your relationship with money. <break time="1.1s" /> “No one can serve two masters. Either you will hate the one and love the other, or you will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 6, verse 24. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus frames it as a question of mastery, not amount. Money is a remarkable tool: it pays your team, funds the mission, builds the product, feeds your family. In your hands it can do enormous good. The trouble starts when the tool climbs into the driver’s seat, when the state of the account sets your mood, when a dip in revenue shakes your identity, when you’d bend a value to protect a margin. That’s the tell that money has quietly become master. A tool serves your purposes; a master dictates them. As a founder you handle more money than most people ever will, and that makes this test sharper, not softer. Practically, keep money in its lane: give regularly so it never feels like yours alone, hold a defined line you won’t cross for profit, and check whether your peace rises and falls with the balance. The goal isn’t to despise money or pretend it doesn’t matter. It’s to keep it as a servant of something higher, deployed toward the kingdom and the good of others, while your true allegiance stays fixed on God. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, show me honestly whether money has become my master. I want it to serve your purposes through my hands, not to rule my heart. Anchor my identity and my peace in you and not in the balance. <break time="1.1s" /> I will make money serve the mission, not master me. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and put your money to work for the kingdom, serving one Master alone. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-m-firstfruits: On Giving the First and Best. <break time="1.8s" /> Notice what comes first when the money arrives, and what only gets what’s left over. <break time="1.1s" /> “Honor the Lord with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops; then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 3, verses 9 to 10. <break time="1.1s" /> Firstfruits meant giving from the top of the harvest, before you knew how the rest of the season would turn out. It was an act of trust, not surplus. For a founder, the modern version is deciding to tithe on business income at the start, before you’ve confirmed the month will cover everything. It’s far easier to promise God the leftovers, to say you’ll give generously once things stabilize. But giving first, off the top, is what actually shapes the heart. It puts God ahead of your fear instead of behind it. This is not a transaction where the first check guarantees overflowing barns on your timeline; Proverbs paints the general pattern of a life ordered rightly, not a vending machine. What giving first really does is reorder your priorities: it declares that the business exists under God, not the other way around, and that provision is his to give. Set the structure so honoring God isn’t left to whatever emotion you feel at month’s end. Decide the percentage, automate it if you can, and give from the first and best rather than the last and least. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I want to honor you with the first of what comes in, not the scraps. Give me the trust to give off the top before I know how the month will land. Reorder my priorities so you come first and my fear comes last. <break time="1.1s" /> I will honor God with the first and best, not the leftovers. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and give from the top of the harvest, trusting the One who sends the rain. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-m-windfall: On a Good Month. <break time="1.8s" /> The deal closed, the month was strong, and it feels good. Pause before you take the credit. <break time="1.1s" /> “But remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you the ability to produce wealth, and so confirms his covenant…” <break time="1.1s" />Deuteronomy 8, verse 18. <break time="1.1s" /> A windfall is a wonderful and dangerous thing. Wonderful, because after the lean months you can finally breathe, pay people well, invest, and give. Dangerous, because success quietly rewrites the story until you believe you built it all by your power and the strength of your hands. Moses warned a people about to prosper: the moment you feel most self-made is exactly when you’re most at risk of forgetting who gave you the ability to produce wealth. Your grit was real. Your late nights were real. And still, the market, the timing, the health to work, the very capacity to create value, all of it was given. Gratitude is the guardrail that keeps a good month from inflating your ego. So celebrate, genuinely; a strong month is a gift meant to be enjoyed, not apologized for. But mark it: give a meaningful portion away while the joy is fresh, thank the people who helped, and remember the God who carried you through the tight months is the same one behind this one. Humility in abundance is harder than faith in scarcity, and just as holy. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> God, thank you for a month that finally broke my way. Guard me from believing I did this alone, when every ability I have came from you. Let my first response to abundance be gratitude and generosity, not pride. <break time="1.1s" /> I will celebrate this gift with gratitude and open hands, not pride. <break time="1.1s" /> Go enjoy the good month humbly, remembering who gave you the strength to earn it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-m-longgame: On the Long Game. <break time="1.8s" /> There’s a shortcut on the table, and it’s glittering. Weigh it against the long, quiet road. <break time="1.1s" /> “Whoever can be trusted with very little can also be trusted with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much.” <break time="1.1s" />Luke 16, verse 10. <break time="1.1s" /> The quick win is seductive because it promises to skip the slow part. The inflated projection, the customer you overpromise, the corner shaved on quality, the deal that trades tomorrow’s trust for today’s cash. It often works, at first. But Jesus ties the small and the large together: how you handle little reveals how you’ll handle much, and character is built in the unglamorous decisions no one applauds. Long-term faithfulness rarely feels heroic. It looks like keeping your word when breaking it would be cheaper, paying vendors on time when you could stall, telling an investor the honest number, doing quiet excellent work for years before anyone notices. This is the harder economy: reputation compounds slowly and collapses fast, and trust, once spent, is expensive to rebuild. The founders who last are usually not the ones who caught the flashiest break but the ones who were faithful in a thousand small, boring, honest moments. Choose the slower road that lets you sleep at night and hand your name to your kids without flinching. Play the long game, because that is the one that actually builds something that lasts. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, the shortcut is tempting and the slow road feels foolish some days. Make me faithful in the small things no one sees, and honest when honesty costs me. Help me build something that lasts rather than grabbing what glitters. <break time="1.1s" /> I will be faithful in the small things and trust God with the long game. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and be faithful in little, for that is where trust with much begins. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-burnout: On Running Empty. <break time="1.8s" /> You were not built to be a bottomless well. Come to the One who is. <break time="1.1s" /> “Do you not know? Have you not heard? The Lord is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He will not grow tired or weary, and his understanding no one can fathom. He gives strength to the weary and increases the power of the weak.” <break time="1.1s" />Isaiah 40, verses 28 to 29. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a kind of tired that sleep doesn’t touch. You’ve been carrying the payroll, the roadmap, the customer who churned, and the voice that says if you stop, it all falls apart. So you push past the warning lights on the dashboard of your own body, because the company can’t afford for you to be human right now. But it can. Isaiah asks the question you keep forgetting: do you not know? The everlasting God does not grow tired or weary — and He gives strength to the weary, precisely to the ones who have run out. Notice He offers strength, not a scolding — He isn’t asking you to quit, but to stop pretending your own well has no bottom when His never runs dry. Your limits are not a design flaw; they are the honest edge of a creature who was never meant to be God. The founder who admits, “I can’t sustain this pace,” is not failing. He is finally telling the truth. Rest is not the reward for finishing. It is the grace that lets you keep going. Lay it down long enough to be reminded that the outcome was never yours to hold alone. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I am tired in places I don’t know how to name. I have been carrying what only You can carry. Give Your strength to my weakness, and let me draw on You today. <break time="1.1s" /> I lay down what I was never meant to hold alone. <break time="1.1s" /> Go gently, and let the God who never tires carry the weight you cannot. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-sabbath: On Keeping a Day. <break time="1.8s" /> God rested not because He was spent, but because the work was good. He invites you into the same trust. <break time="1.1s" /> “By the seventh day God had finished the work he had been doing; so on the seventh day he rested from all his work. Then God blessed the seventh day and made it holy…” <break time="1.1s" />Genesis 2, verses 2 to 3. <break time="1.1s" /> For a founder, a full day of not working can feel like negligence bordering on sin. The inbox keeps filling. Competitors keep shipping. The market never sleeps, so how could you? But Sabbath was God’s idea before it was a commandment, woven into creation itself. He stopped — not because the universe would run itself, but to declare that its running never depended on ceaseless effort. When you keep a day, you preach a sermon to your own anxious heart: the business is not my god, and I am not its. A Sabbath is a weekly act of defiance against the lie that your worth is measured in output. It says the world can turn for twenty-four hours without your hand on the wheel, because it was always His hand underneath. This is hard, practical trust. Close the laptop. Let the notifications pile. Eat a long meal. Walk with people you love. The work will be there Monday, and you will meet it as a person again, not a machine that forgot how to stop. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I confess I have made rest feel reckless. Help me trust that You hold the company while I put it down. Make one day holy in my week again. <break time="1.1s" /> I will stop, and let God be God for a day. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and keep a day, and discover the world still turning in His hands. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-long-middle: On the Long Middle. <break time="1.8s" /> The middle is not a sign you’ve failed. It’s the ground where perseverance is grown. <break time="1.1s" /> “Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.” <break time="1.1s" />Galatians 6, verse 9. <break time="1.1s" /> The beginning had adrenaline. The end will have vindication. But right now you are in the long middle, where the story stopped being exciting and became a grind of the same unglamorous work, done again. Growth is slow. The metrics inch. The people who cheered at your launch have moved on to newer, shinier things, and you are still here, doing good work that no one is applauding. Paul knew this weariness. He doesn’t deny it exists — he names it and then plants a promise underneath it: at the proper time, not your time, the harvest comes. A farmer cannot rush the field. He works soil that shows him nothing for months, trusting a season he cannot see. Your quiet, faithful, unwitnessed days are not wasted; they are seed going into the ground. The temptation of the middle is not usually to quit dramatically — it’s to slowly stop caring. Resist that erosion. Keep doing the good, small thing today. The harvest belongs to those who were still standing when it came. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> God, I am worn down by the sameness of the middle. Renew my hands for good work that no one sees. Help me trust Your timing for the harvest. <break time="1.1s" /> I will keep sowing, even where I cannot yet see the field change. <break time="1.1s" /> Go back to the good work, and do not give up before the season turns. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-comparison: On Watching the Other Lane. <break time="1.8s" /> The race you were given is your own. Run it, and stop timing the runner beside you. <break time="1.1s" /> “We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they are not wise.” <break time="1.1s" />2 Corinthians 10, verse 12. <break time="1.1s" /> A rival raises a round you couldn’t. Another founder trends on the feed while your announcement sinks like a stone. You know their revenue, their headcount, their glossy press — and every number becomes a ruler you hold against yourself. Paul calls this measuring “not wise,” and he’s not being polite. Comparison is a rigged game, because you are weighing your behind-the-scenes against their highlight reel, your full reality against their curated one. It steals joy from real wins and blinds you to the specific work God set in front of you. Your company was not called to be a copy of theirs. The market is wide; God’s provision is not a fixed pie where their slice shrinks yours. When you fix your eyes on the next lane, you drift and stumble in your own. So close the tab. Their story is being written by a Hand you can trust for them too. Yours is being written faithfully, verse by verse, in work only you were placed here to do. Measure your day against your calling, not against a stranger’s press release. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, forgive me for measuring my worth against someone else’s success. Free me from the tab I keep refreshing. Let me run the race You marked out for me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will run my own lane and bless the runners beside me. <break time="1.1s" /> Go eyes forward, content in the work that is yours to do. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-success: On the Danger of Winning. <break time="1.8s" /> Success is a gift to steward, not a trophy to worship. Hold it with open, grateful hands. <break time="1.1s" /> “You may say to yourself, ‘My power and the strength of my hands have produced this wealth for me.’” <break time="1.1s" />Deuteronomy 8, verse 17. <break time="1.1s" /> Adversity has a way of keeping us on our knees. Success is more dangerous, because it whispers that we no longer need to be there. The round closed. The numbers are up and to the right. The room laughs a little louder at your jokes now. And somewhere in that warm glow, a subtle rewrite begins: I did this. My grit, my vision, my strength produced this. Moses warned a people on the edge of prosperity about exactly this forgetting. The peril of the good season is not the money — it’s the amnesia, the quiet erasing of every unearned gift, every open door you didn’t pry open, every talented person who chose to join you. The antidote to pride is not to belittle your work but to remember its source. The same God who sustained you through the lean months is the giver of the fat ones. So let success make you more thankful, not more self-assured; more generous, not more grasping. Name the ability itself as a gift. The founder who remembers where the harvest came from can enjoy it without being ruined by it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, when I am winning, keep me from forgetting You. Every open door, every gift, every strength came from Your hand. Let gratitude guard me from pride. <break time="1.1s" /> I remember the Giver behind every good thing I hold. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and steward your success as a gift, kneeling even on the mountaintop. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-failure: On Learning to Fall. <break time="1.8s" /> A fall is not the end of your story. In God’s hands, even failure becomes instruction. <break time="1.1s" /> “For though the righteous fall seven times, they rise again, but the wicked stumble when calamity strikes.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 24, verse 16. <break time="1.1s" /> The product missed. The launch flopped. The hard call you made turned out wrong, and you’re replaying it at 2 a.m., certain the failure has revealed who you really are. But Scripture assumes the righteous will fall — not once, but seven times. The mark of a faithful person is not an unbroken record; it is the getting back up. Failure feels like a verdict, but in God’s economy it is a teacher, often the only one honest enough to show you what worked in theory but not in reality. What did this cost teach you that success never could? Where did pride, or hurry, or fear steer the decision? Sit with it long enough to learn, but do not build a home there. Shame wants you to conflate what you did with who you are — to say “I failed” and hear “I am a failure.” God untangles the two. He is not surprised by your fall, and He is not finished with you. Grieve the loss honestly, extract the lesson humbly, and then rise. The rising is the righteousness. Tomorrow’s work is waiting for a founder who is wiser now. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, this failure has knocked the wind out of me. Teach me what I need to learn, and separate my mistake from my identity. Give me the courage to rise again. <break time="1.1s" /> I will learn from this fall, and I will rise. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and get up again, wiser and unashamed, held by grace. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-identity: On Who You Are Without It. <break time="1.8s" /> You were a beloved child of God before the company existed, and you will be one long after. <break time="1.1s" /> “But now, this is what the Lord says… ‘Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have summoned you by name; you are mine.’” <break time="1.1s" />Isaiah 43, verse 1. <break time="1.1s" /> Ask a founder who they are, and the pitch comes out before the person does. Somewhere along the way the company stopped being something you do and became who you are. It’s an easy fusion to make when your name is on the deck, your identity on the line with every metric. But it is a fragile place to stand, because it means a bad quarter isn’t just a bad quarter — it’s a referendum on your soul. Hear what God says over you. He summoned you by name, not by title. He calls you His before you shipped a single feature, and He would still call you His if the whole thing folded tomorrow. Your identity is received, not achieved; given by a Father, not earned in a market. This is not less motivating — it is freeing. A founder who knows he is loved apart from the outcome can take real risks, because his worth isn’t riding on them. Let the company be a thing you build, not the thing you are. When you rest your identity in the One who named you, you can lose a deal without losing yourself. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I have let the company become my name. Remind me that I am Yours before I am anything I built. Anchor my worth in Your love, not my results. <break time="1.1s" /> I am God’s before I am anything I have made. <break time="1.1s" /> Go as one who is named and loved, whatever the metrics say. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-finish: On Finishing What You Start. <break time="1.8s" /> Beginnings are easy to love. Faithfulness is proven in the finishing. <break time="1.1s" /> “Suppose one of you wants to build a tower. Won’t you first sit down and estimate the cost to see if you have enough money to complete it?” <break time="1.1s" />Luke 14, verse 28. <break time="1.1s" /> You are a starter. Founders usually are — wired to see the empty lot and imagine the tower. But Jesus points past the thrill of breaking ground to the harder question: can you finish it? Anyone can lay a foundation in a burst of vision. Fewer stay to raise the walls after the novelty wears off, when the launch is old news and what remains is the grinding follow-through of shipping the unglamorous version 1.4, closing the loop, keeping the promise you made to customers and to yourself. Half-built towers dot the landscape of good intentions. There is a quiet integrity in completion — in being the kind of person, and the kind of company, that does what it said it would do. This isn’t about refusing to ever pivot; wisdom counts the cost and sometimes chooses differently. But it is about resisting the founder’s temptation to abandon a nearly-finished thing for a newer, more exciting empty lot. Count the cost, then pay it. Show up for the boring last mile. The world is full of dreamers. Be one of the rarer ones who finishes. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I love beginnings more than endings. Give me the endurance to finish what I have started well. Make me faithful in the unglamorous last mile. <break time="1.1s" /> I will finish the good thing I began. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and complete the tower, faithful to the last stone. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-small-beginnings: On Small Beginnings. <break time="1.8s" /> Do not measure the oak by the acorn. God delights in what starts small. <break time="1.1s" /> “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed … Though it is the smallest of all seeds, yet when it grows, it is the largest of garden plants and becomes a tree…” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 13, verses 31 to 32. <break time="1.1s" /> Ten users. Three hundred dollars in revenue. A single customer who wrote to say your product helped. In a world of billion-dollar headlines, these numbers can feel almost embarrassing to name aloud. You scroll past someone else’s enormous milestone and quietly despise your own small day. But consider how Jesus describes the kingdom: a mustard seed, the smallest thing in the plot, that becomes the largest tree. God is not impressed by size the way the market is. He is the one who hides a whole forest inside a seed and calls it good. Every towering thing you admire was, not long ago, someone’s laughably small beginning. Those first ten users are real people you actually served. That modest revenue is proof the thing works at all. Contempt for small beginnings is really impatience dressed as ambition, and it will rob you of the joy that lives in today’s real, tiny, honest progress. Celebrate the small win out loud. Thank God for the tenth user by name. What He calls the seed of something great, you are allowed to rejoice over too. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I have been ashamed of how small my progress looks. Teach me to see it the way You do — as a seed with a tree hidden inside it. Give me joy in today’s small wins. <break time="1.1s" /> I will celebrate the small beginning that God is growing. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and honor the small day, for great things are hidden inside it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-r-why: On Renewing Your Why. <break time="1.8s" /> When the fire dims, you don’t need a new reason. You need to remember the first one. <break time="1.1s" /> “Yet I hold this against you: You have forsaken the love you had at first. Consider how far you have fallen! Repent and do the things you did at first.” <break time="1.1s" />Revelation 2, verses 4 to 5. <break time="1.1s" /> You didn’t start this for the spreadsheets. Somewhere underneath the funnel metrics and the fundraising theater, there was a first love — a problem that kept you up because you cared, a person you wanted to help, a calling you felt was yours. But somewhere in the grind, the why went quiet. You’re still doing the work, still shipping, but the meaning has leaked out, and you can’t quite remember what you were reaching for. Jesus’ words to a busy, hardworking church are strikingly gentle: you have forsaken your first love. His remedy isn’t to try harder or invent a shinier mission. It’s to remember and return — “do the things you did at first.” Go back to the earliest customer conversation that lit you up. Reread the note you wrote the night you decided to build this. Sit again with the problem itself, not the KPIs around it. A why doesn’t usually die; it gets buried under noise. Dig it back up. When you reconnect the daily work to the love that started it, the same tasks that felt like drudgery this morning can feel like purpose again by tonight. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I have lost sight of why I started. Take me back to the first love that moved me. Reconnect my work to the purpose You planted in me. <break time="1.1s" /> I return to the love that first set me in motion. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and do the things you did at first, with your why alive again. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-focus: On Deep Focus. <break time="1.8s" /> Twelve tabs, three conversations, one half-written thing that actually matters. Before you scatter, gather. <break time="1.1s" /> “Let your eyes look straight ahead; fix your gaze directly before you.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 4, verse 25. <break time="1.1s" /> Your attention has become the most contested real estate you own. Every app on your phone employs brilliant people whose whole job is to pull your eyes sideways, and most days they win. The strange result is that a founder can work ten hours and never once give the business the thing it needs most: a stretch of undivided mind. Proverbs speaks of a fixed gaze — eyes straight ahead, not darting. That’s not a productivity hack; it’s a posture of the heart. Scattered attention usually isn’t a discipline problem so much as a quiet anxiety, a fear that whatever you’re not watching is where the danger is. But you have a Father whose gaze never leaves you, which means you don’t have to monitor everything to be safe. You can close the tabs. You can let the inbox wait an hour. The deepest work you’ll do this week — the hard thinking, the honest writing, the real decision — will happen in the space distraction didn’t get. Guard one block of unbroken attention today and give it to the work that matters. That, too, can be an act of trust. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, my attention is pulled in a hundred directions, and I’m tired of living scattered. Quiet the anxious part of me that keeps checking everything. Teach me to fix my gaze, and let my focused hours today be an offering to you. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give my best work one unbroken hour of full attention today. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into the day with your eyes straight ahead, held by the One whose eyes never leave you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-busyness: On Busyness and Fruit. <break time="1.8s" /> You were in motion all week. Sit still long enough to ask what actually grew. <break time="1.1s" /> “I am the vine; you are the branches. If you remain in me and I in you, you will bear much fruit; apart from me you can do nothing.” <break time="1.1s" />John 15, verse 5. <break time="1.1s" /> Busyness is the most respectable way to be unfruitful. A packed calendar looks like progress, feels like importance, and quietly excuses you from the harder question: is any of this bearing fruit? Founders know the difference in their gut — the week of forty meetings that moved nothing, versus the one quiet morning that changed the company. Jesus doesn’t tell the branches to try harder. He tells them to remain. Fruit, in his picture, is not manufactured by activity; it grows out of connection. A branch straining on its own produces motion, heat, exhaustion — everything but grapes. “Apart from me you can do nothing” is not a scolding; it’s a mercy, because it releases you from the lie that output is generated by sheer velocity. So audit the week the way a gardener would, not the way a timesheet would. What is actually growing — in the product, in your people, in you? Cut one busy thing that bears nothing. Keep the connected things. God is not impressed by your fullest day; he is at work in your fruitful one, and fruit comes from abiding first. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I have mistaken a full schedule for a faithful life. Show me which of my busyness is just motion. Keep me connected to you, the vine, and let what grows from my work this week be real fruit, not noise. <break time="1.1s" /> I will cut one fruitless commitment this week and stay rooted in what actually grows. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and remain in the vine, and let the fruit come from there. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-procrastination: On Putting It Off. <break time="1.8s" /> There it sits, third day on the list — the task you keep organizing around instead of doing. <break time="1.1s" /> “Whoever watches the wind will not plant; whoever looks at the clouds will not reap.” <break time="1.1s" />Ecclesiastes 11, verse 4. <break time="1.1s" /> Procrastination almost never looks like laziness in a founder. It looks like research. It looks like tidying the roadmap, answering easier emails, waiting for the right moment to make the hard call or send the scary draft. Ecclesiastes names the pattern with unsettling precision: the farmer who keeps watching the wind never actually plants anything. He isn’t idle — he’s studying conditions. But the conditions are never quite right, and study has quietly become a place to hide. Under most procrastination sits fear: of doing it badly, of finding out, of being judged by the result. Here is where the gospel loosens the knot. You are not waiting on a perfect performance to be acceptable; you are already accepted, which makes the imperfect first attempt survivable. The draft can be rough. The call can be awkward. Planting is an act of faith precisely because you can’t control the weather — that part has always belonged to God. So name the one task you’ve been circling, and do it first, before the day offers you its usual hiding places. Plant the seed. Let God handle the wind. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you know the task I’ve been avoiding and the fear underneath it. Forgive me for hiding in busywork. Give me the small courage to begin badly rather than wait perfectly, and take charge of the outcomes I can’t control. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do the avoided task first today, before I touch anything easier. <break time="1.1s" /> Go plant today what you have been watching the wind about. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-priorities: On the One Thing. <break time="1.8s" /> Forty items, all marked urgent. Before you triage the list, let the Lord quiet the room. <break time="1.1s" /> “Martha, Martha,” the Lord answered, “you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed — or indeed only one. Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.” <break time="1.1s" />Luke 10, verses 41 to 42. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice that Jesus doesn’t rebuke Martha for working. He names what the work has done to her: worried and upset about many things. That’s the founder’s condition most mornings — not too little to do but too many things claiming to be the thing, until the day is spent reacting and nothing essential moves. Jesus’ answer is almost shockingly narrow: few things are needed, or indeed only one. Mary’s one thing was his presence, and that ordering is the point — when the first priority is sitting with him, the other forty stop shouting with equal authority. From that quiet, a truer question emerges than “what is urgent?” It is: what is needed? If you could move only one thing forward today — one conversation, one decision, one piece of real work — which one would still matter in a month? You usually know. The many things will survive being second. The one thing rarely survives being tenth. Choose it before you open the inbox, and let it take the best hour you have. A day that moves the needed thing is a good day, whatever else goes unfinished. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I am worried and upset about many things, and I confess I like the feeling of being needed by all of them. Sit me down first. Show me the one thing today actually requires, and give me peace about what must wait. <break time="1.1s" /> I will choose the one needed thing before I open the inbox, and give it my best hour. <break time="1.1s" /> Go do the needed thing, and let the many things wait their turn. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-time: On Time as a Gift. <break time="1.8s" /> Another week is gone and you can barely say where. Pause and hold today like something entrusted to you. <break time="1.1s" /> “Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 90, verse 12. <break time="1.1s" /> Founders talk about time the way misers talk about money — saving it, spending it, never having enough of it. But Scripture starts somewhere else: your days are not a possession running out; they are a gift being handed to you, one at a time, by Someone who numbered them before you drew breath. “Teach us to number our days” is not an invitation to panic about the shortness of life. It’s a prayer for wisdom — the settled ability to see a single day at its true value. A steward and a miser handle the same resource differently. The miser grips; the steward invests, and can even give some away without feeling robbed. That reframe changes a calendar. The hour with your kid is not stolen from the company. The unhurried conversation with a struggling teammate is not waste. And the focused morning on the work God gave you is not anxiety’s treadmill; it’s faithful use of a talent entrusted. You cannot make more time, but you were never asked to. You were asked to be found faithful with today. Number it. Spend it on purpose. It was given to you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, every day I have ever lived came from your hand, and I have treated so many of them as raw material. Teach me to number my days rightly. Make me a steward of this one — generous, unhurried, and faithful. <break time="1.1s" /> I will spend today on purpose, as a steward of a gift and not an owner running out. <break time="1.1s" /> Go steward this day well, for it was counted and given to you by God. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-hustle: On the Myth of Hustle. <break time="1.8s" /> The voice says sleep is for the funded and rest is for later. Come listen to a different voice. <break time="1.1s" /> “Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. … In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for food to eat — for he grants sleep to those he loves.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 127, verses 1 to 2. <break time="1.1s" /> Hustle culture preaches a simple gospel: outcomes are purchased with hours, and whoever sleeps least wins. It flatters you, because it makes everything depend on you. Psalm 127 dismantles it in two verses. The psalmist isn’t against building — he assumes you’ll build — but he calls the all-hours version of it vain, and then says something almost scandalous to a founder: God grants sleep to those he loves. Sleep, in this psalm, is not lost productivity. It’s a nightly sermon, preached to your body, that the world is held together by Someone else. The myth of hustle isn’t wrong because hard work is bad; seasons of real push are part of building anything. It’s wrong because it quietly crowns you the sole load-bearing wall of your company, and no human soul is engineered for that weight. You can work hard tomorrow precisely because you are not God tonight. Deals have closed while founders slept. Ideas have arrived in the shower, not the sprint. Do your full day’s work, honestly and well — then put it down, and let the Builder keep building while you rest. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I confess I’ve believed that everything depends on my grind. Unless you build this, I labor in vain. Teach me to work hard and then stop, and to receive sleep as your gift rather than my defeat. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do a full day’s honest work and then put it down, trusting the Builder with the night. <break time="1.1s" /> Go work hard and sleep well, for the Lord builds while you rest. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-finishing: On Finishing What You Start. <break time="1.8s" /> The exciting part is over and only the finishing is left — the unglamorous miles where most things quietly die. <break time="1.1s" /> “Now finish the work, so that your eager willingness to do it may be matched by your completion of it, according to your means.” <break time="1.1s" />2 Corinthians 8, verse 11. <break time="1.1s" /> Starting is intoxicating. The blank repo, the fresh deck, the whiteboard full of possibility — beginnings run on inspiration, and inspiration is cheap. Finishing runs on something costlier. The Corinthians had eagerly pledged a gift and then let it stall, and Paul’s counsel is bracingly practical: let your completion match your willingness. He’s naming a gap every founder knows — between the enthusiasm that starts things and the fidelity that ships them. Your half-done projects aren’t failures of talent; they’re usually the moment when the work stopped feeding your excitement and started requiring your faithfulness. But notice the mercy in Paul’s phrase “according to your means.” God is not demanding a heroic finish beyond what you have. He’s asking you to close the loop with what is actually in your hands — the feature at ninety percent, the hire half-onboarded, the hard conversation opened and never landed. Shipping is a form of keeping your word, to your customers and to your earlier self. Pick one unfinished thing this week and carry it all the way across the line. Done, it can finally serve someone. Almost done, it serves no one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I am quick to begin and slow to complete. Forgive the trail of almost-finished things behind me. Give me the humble endurance of the last mile, and help me ship what I said I would. <break time="1.1s" /> I will take one nearly-finished thing all the way across the line this week. <break time="1.1s" /> Go finish the work, so your completion matches your willingness. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-margin: On Margin. <break time="1.8s" /> Look at your calendar: wall-to-wall color, not one blank hour. Even Jesus looked at days like that and said, come away. <break time="1.1s" /> “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” <break time="1.1s" />Mark 6, verse 31. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus said this on a day when so many people were coming and going that his team had no chance even to eat. It was, by any founder’s measure, traction — demand exceeding capacity, the mission working. And his response to that momentum was to schedule white space. We treat margin as the leftover, the slack we’ll enjoy once things calm down. But a page printed edge to edge is unreadable, and a life scheduled edge to edge is unlivable — there’s no room for the unexpected customer crisis, the teammate who needs twenty unhurried minutes, the idea that only surfaces when you’re not producing. Margin isn’t the enemy of productivity; it’s the condition for the kind that lasts. An engine at redline makes impressive noise and doesn’t last the year. Notice, too, that Jesus doesn’t send the disciples off alone; he says come with me. The quiet place isn’t just recovery — it’s company with him, the kind you can’t keep at a sprint. So put white space on the calendar with the same seriousness you give a board meeting. It is not empty. It’s where the best of you gets restored. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, my week has no room in it, and I have called that success. Teach me to guard margin the way I guard revenue. Draw me into the quiet place with you, and restore what the pace has worn thin. <break time="1.1s" /> I will block real white space in this week’s calendar and defend it like a commitment. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and keep some blank space in your days, for that is where you will hear him. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-from-rest: On Working from Rest. <break time="1.8s" /> You keep telling yourself you can rest once the work is done. But the work of a founder is never done — so the rest never starts. <break time="1.1s" /> “There remains, then, a Sabbath-rest for the people of God; for anyone who enters God’s rest also rests from their works, just as God did from his.” <break time="1.1s" />Hebrews 4, verses 9 to 10. <break time="1.1s" /> Most founders work for rest: push through the sprint, close the round, hit the milestone — and then, finally, exhale. Except the exhale keeps moving. There is always a next milestone, so rest becomes a country you’re always emigrating toward and never reach. Scripture runs the sequence the other way around. In Genesis, humanity is created on the sixth day, which means our first full day of existence was God’s day of rest — we woke up into completion we hadn’t earned. Hebrews makes the pattern explicit: entering God’s rest means resting from your own works as the ground of your standing. That is the gospel applied to a calendar. You are not laboring toward acceptance; you are laboring from it. The verdict on you was settled at the cross, not at the quarter’s close. This changes the texture of a workweek more than any productivity system. Work done to earn rest is anxious, grasping, impossible to put down. Work done from rest can be bold, generous, and finished at a reasonable hour — because nothing ultimate is riding on it. Begin today already accepted. Then go build. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I have been working to earn a peace you already gave me. Settle my heart in what is finished before I touch what is unfinished. Let me build from your rest today, not toward it. <break time="1.1s" /> I will start today from acceptance already given, not work toward a rest I must earn. <break time="1.1s" /> Go to your work from his rest, as one already loved and already received. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-w-today: On Doing Today’s Work Today. <break time="1.8s" /> Half your mind is on next quarter, next raise, next risk. Bring it back to the one day you’ve actually been given. <break time="1.1s" /> “Then the Lord said to Moses, ‘I will rain down bread from heaven for you. The people are to go out each day and gather enough for that day …’” <break time="1.1s" />Exodus 16, verse 4. <break time="1.1s" /> A founder’s mind lives in the future by trade — modeling scenarios, gaming out the raise, rehearsing the churn that hasn’t happened yet. Some of that is planning, and planning is wisdom. But there’s a point where planning curdles into pre-suffering: you carry tomorrow’s troubles today, without tomorrow’s grace, because grace, like manna, is given a day at a time. The manna instruction is strikingly concrete: go out each day and gather enough for that day. God isn’t promising an easy tomorrow; he’s pointing out that you’ve been issued exactly one day of bread, and it’s for this one. The practical shape of that trust is almost embarrassingly simple — do today’s work today. Write the code in front of you. Make today’s calls. Solve the problem that actually exists rather than the six that might. You will handle next month’s crisis next month, with resources that haven’t been given yet and help you can’t currently see, because the Father who feeds you today will still be there when tomorrow becomes today. Anxiety splits you between two days and does justice to neither. Faith gathers you into one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I keep living a week ahead of my own life. Forgive my borrowing of troubles you haven’t assigned to me. Give me this day’s bread and this day’s work, and I will leave tomorrow in your hands. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do today’s work today and leave tomorrow’s troubles for tomorrow’s grace. <break time="1.1s" /> Go live this one day fully, and let tomorrow wait for you in the Father’s hands. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-l-weight: On the Weight of Payroll. <break time="1.8s" /> You approved payroll again this week — a list of names, and behind every name a rent check, a grocery run, a kid’s shoes. Sit with that for a moment before you rush past it. <break time="1.1s" /> “Masters, provide your slaves with what is right and fair, because you know that you also have a Master in heaven.” <break time="1.1s" />Colossians 4, verse 1. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a particular weight that only employers know: the knowledge that real households eat because your company works. It can keep you up at night, and in a strange way it should — not as dread, but as reverence. Paul’s word to masters cuts both directions at once. First, the responsibility is real: provide what is right and fair. Your people’s dependence on you is not a burden to resent or leverage to exploit; it is a trust to honor, and honoring it — the fair wage, the honest review, the benefits you didn’t have to offer — is a form of worship. But the second half of the verse carries the mercy: you also have a Master in heaven. You are not the last link in the chain. The same God who feeds sparrows feeds your team, and he was providing for every one of those families long before you hired them. So carry the weight, but carry it as a steward, not a savior. Their paychecks pass through your hands; their provision rests in his. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, thank you for trusting me with people whose livelihoods run through this company. Keep me honest and generous with what passes through my hands. And when the weight feels like more than I can hold, remind me that I am a steward and you are the Provider. <break time="1.1s" /> I will treat this week’s payroll as a trust from God, and pray by name for the people on it. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and provide what is right and fair, remembering that you too are provided for. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-l-conflict: On Standing Between Two People. <break time="1.8s" /> Two people you hired, both good at their jobs, can no longer work together — and the meeting where you sit between them is on your calendar. You don’t get to skip it. <break time="1.1s" /> “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 5, verse 9. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice that Jesus blesses peacemakers, not peacekeepers. A peacekeeper manages appearances: reroutes the Slack channels, reshuffles the project teams, hopes the tension starves quietly in the dark. A peacemaker walks into the middle of it. That is what the mediation meeting really is — not an HR chore, but a small act of family resemblance, because making peace between estranged parties is what your Father does. He did it for you, at cost, when you were the one at odds with him. So go in the way he does: hear each person fully before you judge, name the real issue instead of the polite one, and refuse to let either party leave as the villain. You are not there to declare a winner; you are there to make it possible for two image-bearers to work side by side again. It may take more than one conversation. It will certainly take more courage than avoidance would have. But when you stand in the gap between two people, you stand where Christ stood, and Jesus says that ground is blessed. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you made peace with me when I was the difficult party, so I have no excuse for avoiding this. Give me ears that hear both sides honestly and a heart that refuses to pick a favorite. Make me an agent of real peace, not managed silence. <break time="1.1s" /> I will stop rerouting around this conflict and schedule the honest conversation it requires. <break time="1.1s" /> Go stand between them without fear, for peacemakers bear the family name of God. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-l-feedback: On Wounds That Can Be Trusted. <break time="1.8s" /> You’ve rewritten the opening line of that conversation a dozen times, hoping a softer phrasing will make it stop being hard. It won’t. Say the true thing. <break time="1.1s" /> “Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 27, verses 5 to 6. <break time="1.1s" /> The Proverbs make a claim that feels backwards until you’ve lived it: withheld truth is a form of withheld love. When you know an employee is underperforming and you say nothing — when the performance review is all sanded edges and the one-on-one stays safely on logistics — it can feel like kindness. Scripture calls it hidden love, and ranks it below open rebuke. Because here is what your silence actually does: it lets someone walk further down a road that ends badly, while you protect yourself from an awkward hour. The flattering enemy multiplies kisses; the faithful friend risks the wound. But notice the condition — wounds from a friend can be trusted. Your feedback earns trust the same way: given in private, aimed at the work and not the soul, delivered by someone who has clearly already decided to keep believing in them. That is how God deals with you — honest about your sin, unwavering in his love, never one without the other. Go into that conversation as his apprentice. Say the hard thing plainly, and stay in the room while it lands. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you have never flattered me, and you have never abandoned me — teach me to offer both truths together. Take away my cowardice that dresses up as kindness. Give me plain words and a warm heart for this conversation, and let the wound I must give be one that heals. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give the honest feedback I have been softening into silence, with kindness and without delay. <break time="1.1s" /> Go speak the truth like a friend, and trust God with how it lands. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-l-developing: On Seeing What Someone Could Become. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere on your team is a person doing good work a size too small for them. You’ve noticed. Have you told them? <break time="1.1s" /> “And the things you have heard me say in the presence of many witnesses entrust to reliable people who will also be qualified to teach others.” <break time="1.1s" />2 Timothy 2, verse 2. <break time="1.1s" /> Paul looked at Timothy — young, timid, prone to self-doubt — and saw a man who could carry churches. Then he did the thing that actually develops people: he entrusted. Not after Timothy felt ready; Timothy never felt ready. Paul handed him real weight and stayed close while he learned to bear it. That is the pattern, and it costs the leader something every time. Delegating a stretch project to someone unproven is slower than doing it yourself, and riskier than giving it to your safest hands. But a company where nothing is ever entrusted is a company where no one ever grows, and a leader who hoards the hard jobs is quietly telling the team he doesn’t believe in them. You became who you are because someone gave you a chance you hadn’t fully earned — and behind that someone stands a God who routinely calls people by what they will become, not what they currently are. Simon becomes Peter, the rock, long before he acts like one. Look at your team the way God looked at you. Then entrust. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you called me before I was ready and grew me through what you dared to entrust to me. Give me eyes to see who on my team is standing where I once stood. Make me generous with opportunity and patient with the wobbles that come with it. <break time="1.1s" /> I will hand one person a responsibility this month that is bigger than their current job, and stay close while they grow into it. <break time="1.1s" /> Go entrust something real to someone unproven, as God once did with you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-l-culture: On Culture Under Pressure. <break time="1.8s" /> The deadline is brutal, the Slack messages are getting shorter, and the jokes have stopped. Everyone is watching one person to learn how to act right now — and that person is you. <break time="1.1s" /> “Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Thessalonians 5, verse 11. <break time="1.1s" /> Culture is not what the values slide says; it is how people treat each other on the worst week of the quarter. Paul wrote to a young church under real pressure — hostility outside, anxiety about the future inside — and his instruction was strikingly ordinary: encourage one another, build each other up. Not once the pressure lifts. In it. Because encouragement is not a luxury for calm seasons; it is load-bearing structure for hard ones. When a team is stressed, everything unspoken gets read in the darkest light — the terse message, the canceled one-on-one, the meeting that ran silent. Your job as the leader is to keep saying what pressure tries to silence: that the work matters, that you see the effort, that a missed target is a problem to solve and not a verdict on anyone’s worth. Notice, too, that Paul makes it mutual — one another. You cannot carry the whole team’s morale alone, but you can be the first voice, and first voices set cultures. The gospel frees you for this: your people’s standing does not rise and fall with the sprint, and neither does yours. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, when I am stressed, my team feels it before I admit it. Guard my tone in the crunch, and put encouraging words in my mouth when the pressure tempts me toward silence or sharpness. Build in us a culture that holds under weight. <break time="1.1s" /> I will send one specific, genuine word of encouragement to each person on my team before the week ends. <break time="1.1s" /> Go be the first encouraging voice in a stressed room, and watch others find theirs. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-3am: On the 3am Wake-Up. <break time="1.8s" /> You know the hour — awake in the dark, the whole company pressing down before the alarm has any right to ring. Bring that hour here. <break time="1.1s" /> “In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, Lord, make me dwell in safety.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 4, verse 8. <break time="1.1s" /> The 3am version of your company is never the true one. In the dark, the runway is always shorter, the churn always steeper, the email you haven’t answered always fatal. Night strips away proportion and leaves only dread, and dread does math badly. David wrote this psalm with real enemies circling — not imagined ones — and still he ends the day the same way: he lies down, and he sleeps. Notice why. Not because the situation resolved. Because “you alone, Lord, make me dwell in safety.” His rest was not a verdict on his circumstances; it was a verdict on his God. Here is the quiet arithmetic of grace: the world is not held together by your vigilance. It never was. While you sleep, God does not — payroll, pipeline, and all the unfinished things sit in hands stronger than yours. The 3am wake-up believes you are the last line of defense. The gospel says a Father is on watch, and the watchman’s shift was never yours. You are allowed to lie back down. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you know the hour I wake and what waits for me there. Take the weight I keep picking up in the dark. Remind me that you are awake so I don’t have to be. Give me the sleep you give to those you love. <break time="1.1s" /> I will hand God the 3am list and go back to sleep, because keeping watch is his work, not mine. <break time="1.1s" /> Lie down in peace tonight — the One who holds your company does not sleep. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-metrics: On Opening the Dashboard. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you open the dashboard or the inbox, pause. Notice the bracing in your body — and bring it to God first. <break time="1.1s" /> “They will have no fear of bad news; their hearts are steadfast, trusting in the Lord.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 112, verse 7. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a particular flinch founders know: the half-second before the metrics load, before the inbox refreshes, when anything could be waiting. A churned account. An investor’s cold reply. A red line on the revenue chart. You check compulsively, hoping to catch bad news before it catches you — as if speed were safety. The psalmist describes a different kind of person: not one who never receives bad news, but one who has no fear of it. Read that carefully. The promise is not a clean dashboard. The promise is a steadfast heart. Steadfastness doesn’t come from the numbers being good; it comes from something truer than the numbers — a God whose care for you does not refresh with the page. Bad news, when it comes, will arrive inside his providence, not outside it. That means you can look at the dashboard instead of bracing against it. The data is information, not identity, and certainly not verdict. Your standing before God was settled at the cross, and no metric loads with the power to change it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you see how I flinch before the numbers load. Settle my heart in something steadier than a chart. Let me receive whatever today’s news is — good or hard — inside your care. Make my heart steadfast, trusting in you. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pray before I check, so the first voice I hear today is God’s and not the dashboard’s. <break time="1.1s" /> Open the day unafraid — no news can reach you outside the reach of God. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-peace: On a Peace the World Can’t Give. <break time="1.8s" /> Ask yourself honestly: when were you last at peace, and what made it so? Sit with the answer for a moment. <break time="1.1s" /> “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid.” <break time="1.1s" />John 14, verse 27. <break time="1.1s" /> Most of what founders call peace is really just good conditions: the round closed, the numbers up, the team stable, Slack quiet. It feels like peace, but it is weather — and weather changes. That is what Jesus means by peace “as the world gives”: conditional, circumstantial, gone the moment the conditions go. Notice when he offered the other kind. It was the night before the cross, hours from betrayal and death, everything by any measure falling apart. That is when he said, “my peace I give you.” His peace was not the absence of trouble; it was the presence of the Father inside it. This is what he hands to you — not a promise that the metrics will hold, but himself, unchanging, in whatever the metrics do. A peace anchored in circumstances is a peace your circumstances can repossess. A peace anchored in Christ is yours in the up round and the down round alike. Stop waiting for the business to be calm before you are. He is offering something the business was never able to give you anyway. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Jesus, my peace has been tied to conditions — and my conditions keep changing. Give me the peace you promised, the kind the world cannot give or take. Anchor my heart in you and not in the weather of this company. Let me be calm because you are near. <break time="1.1s" /> I will stop outsourcing my peace to my circumstances and receive it from Christ instead. <break time="1.1s" /> Go in the peace that was given on the hardest night in history — it will hold on your hard days too. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-catastrophe: On the Stories Fear Tells. <break time="1.8s" /> Catch the story you’ve been telling yourself — the one that starts with a bad email and ends with the company gone. Bring the whole story here. <break time="1.1s" /> “When anxiety was great within me, your consolation brought me joy.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 94, verse 19. <break time="1.1s" /> Anxiety is a gifted novelist. Give it one lost deal and it will draft the whole tragedy: the miss becomes a trend, the trend becomes a death spiral, the death spiral becomes the day you tell the team it’s over. You’ve lived that story a hundred times, and it has come true almost never. The psalmist knew this crowding of the mind — “when anxiety was great within me” is literally when my anxious thoughts multiplied. He doesn’t deny them or argue each one down. He lets a different voice in: “your consolation brought me joy.” Consolation is not information; it is presence. God rarely answers catastrophizing with a forecast. He answers it with himself — the steady reminder that whatever chapter comes, you will not be in it alone, and the ending is not fear’s to write. The cross is proof that God can be authoring redemption inside a scene that looks like total loss. So let fear finish its draft, then put it down. It is fiction. Your actual future is held by Someone kinder than your imagination. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, my anxious thoughts multiply faster than I can answer them. When fear writes its endings, interrupt me with your consolation. Remind me that you hold the future my imagination keeps trying to hold. Bring me back to what is actually true today. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name fear’s story as fiction and answer it with what God has actually said. <break time="1.1s" /> Put down the tragedy fear drafted — the Author of your story is not anxious about the ending. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-alone: On Carrying It Alone. <break time="1.8s" /> Feel the weight you walked in with — payroll, the roadmap, every person counting on you. You were never meant to carry it by yourself. <break time="1.1s" /> “Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Peter 5, verse 7. <break time="1.1s" /> Founders carry a strange loneliness. The team looks to you, the investors look to you, even your family looks to you — and there is no one above you on the org chart to look to. So you absorb it all: the payroll that must clear, the pivot that must work, the futures of everyone who took a chance on this. It feels noble. It is actually crushing, and it was never the design. Peter’s word “cast” is not gentle; it is the verb for heaving a load off your back onto something built to bear it — the same word used for throwing cloaks onto a donkey before Jesus rode it. And the reason given is not that God is strong, though he is. It is that he cares for you. Not for your company first — for you. The weight you carry alone is a weight he has already offered to take, and carrying it anyway is not faithfulness; it is just exhaustion wearing faithfulness’s clothes. There is someone above you after all. Heave it over. He has been waiting for the handoff. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I have been carrying this company as if there were no one above me. Today I cast it onto you — the payroll, the people, the pressure. Thank you that you care for me, not just for what I build. Teach me to keep handing it back. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name the heaviest thing I’m carrying today and deliberately hand it to God in prayer. <break time="1.1s" /> Go lighter — the load was his to carry, and he cares for you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-crisis: On the Moment of Panic. <break time="1.8s" /> Maybe the crisis is now — the outage, the resignation, the wire that didn’t land. Take one slow breath before anything else. Christ is in this boat. <break time="1.1s" /> “The disciples woke him and said to him, ‘Teacher, don’t you care if we drown?’ He got up, rebuked the wind and said to the waves, ‘Quiet! Be still!’ Then the wind died down and it was completely calm.” <break time="1.1s" />Mark 4, verses 38 to 39. <break time="1.1s" /> Every founder has a storm story: the server down during the launch, the lead investor pulling out at the eleventh hour, the co-founder’s resignation letter. In the moment, panic feels like the only rational response — the disciples were experienced fishermen, and even they were sure they were drowning. Their accusation is the one we all pray in a crisis: don’t you care? And notice what the story actually says: Jesus was in the boat the whole time. Asleep, yes — but present, unbothered, and entirely unthreatened by the thing that was undoing them. The storm’s size had not changed his authority over it. When he speaks, the sea that seemed ultimate turns out to be obedient. Your crisis is real; this story never pretends storms aren’t wet and violent. But it insists on a deeper fact: nothing happening to you right now is happening outside the presence and authority of Christ. Panic says you are alone in the boat with the storm. The gospel says the storm is in the boat with him. Do the next right thing — but do it as someone accompanied. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, this feels like drowning, and my honest prayer is the disciples’ prayer: don’t you care? Thank you that you are in this boat and not shaken by what shakes me. Speak your peace over this crisis and over my chest. Steady me for the next right step. <break time="1.1s" /> I will handle this crisis as someone whose boat carries Christ, taking the next step without the panic. <break time="1.1s" /> Face the storm accompanied — the wind and waves still answer to the One beside you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-lowgrade: On the Hum of Worry. <break time="1.8s" /> Not every anxiety is a crisis. Some is just a hum under everything — the low static of running a company. Turn the volume down and listen for God instead. <break time="1.1s" /> “Look at the birds of the air; they do not sow or reap or store away in barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they?” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 6, verse 26. <break time="1.1s" /> The worry that wears founders down is rarely the dramatic kind. It is the hum: the background process always running, quietly consuming cycles — cash, hiring, the competitor’s launch, the thing you forgot. You can work through it, laugh through it, even pray through it, and it never quite switches off. Notice how practical Jesus is about this. He doesn’t rebuke; he redirects. Look at the birds, he says — actually look. It is a strange prescription: interrupt the hum with observation. The birds have no barns, no reserves, no eighteen-month runway, and they are fed, because a Father is providing in ten thousand quiet ways no bird ever tracks. Then the gentle argument: are you not much more valuable than they? Your Father’s provision is not a resource you might exhaust; it is an overflow of how he regards you. The hum of worry is, underneath everything, a doubt about that regard. So the treatment is not trying harder to relax. It is looking — at birds, at every past month he carried you — until the static gives way to trust. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, quiet the hum in me — the low worry that never fully stops. Teach me to interrupt it by looking at your provision instead of my projections. Thank you for every month you have already carried me. Let trust become my background process. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pause once today, look at how God has provided so far, and let that quiet the static. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and look at the birds — you are worth far more to your Father than they. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-perception: On What They Think of You. <break time="1.8s" /> You replayed the all-hands. You reread your own Slack message twice before sending. Come away from the mirror of other people’s eyes for a few minutes. <break time="1.1s" /> “Am I now trying to win the approval of human beings, or of God? Or am I trying to please people? If I were still trying to please people, I would not be a servant of Christ.” <break time="1.1s" />Galatians 1, verse 10. <break time="1.1s" /> Leadership puts you on a stage you never fully leave. Every decision is watched, every mood interpreted; you find yourself wondering what the team said after the meeting ended, whether the new hire is already disappointed, whether they can tell you’re improvising. Caring about your people is good. Being governed by their imagined verdicts is a quiet captivity — and Paul names the stakes plainly: you cannot be enslaved to human approval and free to serve Christ at the same time. One audience will always outrank the other. Here is the release the gospel offers: the only opinion with final authority over you has already been rendered, and it was rendered at the cross, where God looked at you fully known — flaws, improvisation, and all — and chose you. That verdict does not fluctuate with your team’s morale. Paradoxically, this frees you to lead them better. A founder desperate to be liked cannot say hard things, make unpopular calls, or admit mistakes. A founder already approved by God can. Serve your people deeply. Perform for them never. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I confess how much I orbit other people’s opinions of me. Free me from leading for their approval, and let me lead from yours. You have already rendered the verdict that matters. Make me secure enough in it to serve honestly. <break time="1.1s" /> I will make today’s decisions before an audience of One, and serve my team instead of performing for them. <break time="1.1s" /> Lead as one already approved — the verdict over your life came down at the cross, and it was mercy. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-outcomes: On Handing Over the Outcome. <break time="1.8s" /> The pitch is sent. The launch is live. The offer is out. There is nothing left to do but wait — which is exactly where this moment finds you. <break time="1.1s" /> “I planted the seed, Apollos watered it, but God has been making it grow. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Corinthians 3, verses 6 to 7. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a line in every venture where your agency ends. You can write the deck, but not the investor’s yes. You can ship the feature, but not the adoption curve. You can make the offer, but not the acceptance. Most founder anxiety lives on the far side of that line — straining at outcomes as if enough worry could reach across and move them. Paul draws the line cleanly. Planting is yours. Watering is yours. Growth belongs to God, and it never changes hands. This is not an excuse for passivity; Paul planted with everything he had. It is a job description with a boundary, and the boundary is grace. Do the work in front of you with full effort and honest craft — then open your hands, because the part you’re clenching over was never in them. The farmer who has sown and watered does not sit in the field yelling at the soil. He goes home and sleeps, because the mystery of growth belongs to Someone else. Your metrics may rise or fall this quarter. Either way, you will have done your part — and God will not have forgotten his. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I have done the work, and now I am clenched around the result. I open my hands and give the outcome to you. Growth was always yours to give, not mine to force. Let me rest tonight as one who planted faithfully. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do today’s work with full effort and then name the outcome out loud as God’s, not mine. <break time="1.1s" /> Plant and water with all your heart — then leave the growing to God, and go home. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-a-stillness: On Stillness as a Discipline. <break time="1.8s" /> Nothing in your calendar will make you be still today. It has to be chosen. Choose it now, for these few minutes. <break time="1.1s" /> “Be still, and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 46, verse 10. <break time="1.1s" /> To a founder, stillness feels like a luxury at best and negligence at worst. Every quiet minute is a minute the competitor is shipping, the inbox is filling, the market is moving. So we treat stillness as what happens when the work runs out — which means it never happens at all. But this psalm is not a spa slogan; it is a command issued in the middle of upheaval, in a psalm full of roaring waters and tottering kingdoms. Be still. Stop. Drop your hands. And the reason follows: and know that I am God — which carries a quiet second clause: and you are not. Stillness is how that knowledge gets past your calendar and into your bones. It is a discipline precisely because it is an argument: every chosen pause declares that the world will not collapse without your motion, that God’s exaltation does not depend on your quarter. The founder who cannot stop is not proving devotion; he is revealing what he believes holds everything up. Practice stopping — daily, briefly, stubbornly. It will feel like falling behind. It is actually falling into place. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> God, stillness frightens me — it feels like losing ground. But you command it, so it must be safe. Teach me to stop long enough to remember that you are God and I am not. Build this discipline into my days until it becomes rest. <break time="1.1s" /> I will schedule ten unhurried minutes of stillness today and keep them like an investor meeting. <break time="1.1s" /> Be still today, even briefly — the world is held up by God, and he was never in a hurry. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-incomplete: On Deciding Without the Whole Map. <break time="1.8s" /> The deck is built, the diligence is done, and the one thing you still don’t have is certainty. You have to choose anyway. <break time="1.1s" /> “As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the body is formed in a mother’s womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things. Sow your seed in the morning, and at evening let your hands not be idle, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or whether both will do equally well.” <break time="1.1s" />Ecclesiastes 11, verses 5 to 6. <break time="1.1s" /> Every founder decision is made in fog.
