The market analysis is a guess dressed in a spreadsheet; the hiring loop is four hours of conversation standing in for four years of partnership; the term sheet prices a future no one has seen. Solomon did not respond to this fog by demanding certainty. He named it — you do not know the path of the wind — and then, astonishingly, told you to sow anyway. Morning and evening, this field and that one, precisely because you do not know which will succeed. Wisdom, it turns out, is not the elimination of ignorance. It is faithfulness inside it. You are not the Maker of all things, and the gospel makes that good news rather than an accusation: the One who does understand the work has already secured the ending, which frees you to act in the middle of the story. So gather what facts you can, honestly and without stalling. Then decide. The outcome was never the part God assigned to you. The sowing was. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I keep waiting to feel sure, and sure never comes. Thank You that You understand the work I cannot see and that my not-knowing is no threat to Your plans. Give me the honesty to gather what I can and the courage to decide with the light I have. Keep my hands sowing while You keep the harvest. <break time="1.1s" /> I will make this decision with the information I have and entrust the outcome to God. <break time="1.1s" /> Go sow your seed in the morning, and leave the wind to its Maker. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-counsel: On Counsel and Conviction. <break time="1.8s" /> You’ve asked five smart people about the same decision and gotten five confident answers. Somewhere in the noise, your own conviction has gone quiet. <break time="1.1s" /> “Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 15, verse 22. <break time="1.1s" /> Scripture is unembarrassed about advice. Plans fail for lack of counsel; with many advisers they succeed. So ask. Call the founder two years ahead of you, the operator who has run this play, the friend who knew you before the company did. But notice what advisers do in Proverbs: they inform the plan. They do not carry it. There is a version of seeking counsel that is really a search for someone to decide for you — polling investors, mentors, and your group chat until a majority forms and you can hide inside it. That is not humility; it is a way of outsourcing responsibility, and it will leave you leading a company by referendum. Wise counsel works differently. It stress-tests the conviction God has been forming in you; it exposes blind spots, questions assumptions, and then hands the decision back. Christ has already secured your standing, which means a wrong call cannot unmake you — so you are free to listen openly and still decide alone. Gather many advisers. Then close the laptop and choose, as the steward the decision actually belongs to. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, thank You for the wise people You have placed around me; help me hear them without hiding behind them. Show me where I am collecting opinions to avoid the weight of deciding. Form real conviction in me, and give me the spine to act on it. I would rather be responsible before You than comfortable in the crowd. <break time="1.1s" /> I will seek honest counsel this week and then make the call myself, without polling for permission. <break time="1.1s" /> Go listen widely, decide singly, and carry the call with a clear conscience. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-slowyes: On the Slow Yes and the Quick No. <break time="1.8s" /> The opportunity is shiny and the window feels short. Before you say yes, remember what a yes actually costs. <break time="1.1s" /> “The plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 21, verse 5. <break time="1.1s" /> Every yes you give is a bundle of hidden yeses: yes to the meetings it spawns, the roadmap it bends, the people it will require, the quieter work it will quietly starve. That is why the wise are slow with their yes. Proverbs draws the line plainly — the plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty. Haste is not speed; plenty of godly decisions are fast. Haste is speed without counting, the yes given because the offer flattered you or the fear of missing out outran the math. The quick no is different. A no can be given in a day, kindly and cleanly, because a no costs you one possibility while a careless yes mortgages a hundred. Here is the freedom underneath the discipline: you are not scrambling for your one shot. Your future is not so fragile that it hinges on catching every passing opportunity; it rests with a Father who holds tomorrow. So let the diligent plan breathe. Say no quickly, say yes slowly, and let the yeses you do give have your whole heart. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I feel the pull of every open door and the fear of watching one close. Settle me enough to count the cost before I commit. Give me kindness for my quick nos and patience for my slow yeses. I trust You with the opportunities I let pass. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give this decision the time it deserves and decline quickly what I already know is not mine. <break time="1.1s" /> Go guard your yes, spend it slowly, and let it be whole when you give it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-doors: On Two Kinds of Doors. <break time="1.8s" /> Some doors swing both ways; some lock behind you. The first question of a prudent founder is which kind you’re standing in front of. <break time="1.1s" /> “The simple believe anything, but the prudent give thought to their steps.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 14, verse 15. <break time="1.1s" /> Not all decisions deserve the same weight, and treating them as if they do is its own kind of foolishness. The prudent give thought to their steps — and part of that thought is asking what kind of step this is. A pricing test, a landing page, a process you can unwind next quarter: those doors swing both ways, and wisdom walks through them quickly, because the cheapest teacher is a reversible mistake. But a cofounder, a lead investor on your cap table, a name on a five-year lease, a culture you let calcify — those doors tend to lock behind you. They deserve slowness, counsel, prayer, and the humility to imagine being wrong. Much founder anguish comes from inverting this: agonizing for weeks over the reversible while signing the irreversible in a rush of momentum. Sort your doors first. And take heart in this: even the locked doors of your past are not beyond God. The gospel is the story of a God who redeems what cannot be undone. Prudence asks the question beforehand precisely because grace should not be presumed upon — but the grace is real. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, teach me to tell my doors apart. Make me quick where mistakes are cheap and slow where they are permanent. Guard me from rushing the choices that will outlive my attention span. And thank You that even my locked doors are not locked to You. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name which of my current decisions are reversible and which are not, and weight my time accordingly. <break time="1.1s" /> Go step boldly through the doors that swing, and kneel before the ones that lock. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-bothgood: On Choosing Between Two Goods. <break time="1.8s" /> You’ve prayed, you’ve listed the pros, and the honest verdict is that either path would be faithful. The agony is that no one will make this choice for you. <break time="1.1s" /> “The Lord makes firm the steps of the one who delights in him; though he may stumble, he will not fall, for the Lord upholds him with his hand.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 37, verses 23 to 24. <break time="1.1s" /> Some decisions have no wrong answer, and those can be the hardest of all. Two strong candidates. Two good markets. Two faithful ways to spend the next year of your one life. You keep waiting for God to break the tie, and heaven stays quiet — not because He has abandoned you, but because He may be honoring you. The psalm does not say the Lord dictates the steps of the one who delights in him; it says He makes them firm. Delight comes first, then steps — your steps, freely chosen — and then a promise that covers both outcomes: though he may stumble, he will not fall, for the Lord upholds him with his hand. God is not hiding the right envelope behind His back, waiting to grade you. When both roads are good, the choice itself is a gift, the kind a father gives a child he is teaching to walk. So delight in Him. Then pick — actually pick — and walk. The firmness under your feet was never the correctness of your choice. It was always His hand. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I have asked You to choose for me, and I sense You handing the choice back with love. Thank You that Your grip on me does not depend on picking perfectly. Help me delight in You more than I fear a wrong turn. I will choose, and I will trust You to make my steps firm. <break time="1.1s" /> I will stop waiting for a tiebreaker, choose one good path, and walk it wholeheartedly. <break time="1.1s" /> Go choose freely, walk firmly, and let the Lord’s hand be your safety. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-pressure: On Deciding Under Pressure. <break time="1.8s" /> The term sheet expires Friday and the candidate has a competing offer. Someone built a countdown into your decision, and your pulse is starting to do the deciding. <break time="1.1s" /> “So this is what the Sovereign Lord says: ‘See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone for a sure foundation; the one who relies on it will never be stricken with panic.’” <break time="1.1s" />Isaiah 28, verse 16. <break time="1.1s" /> Pressure is a solvent; it dissolves judgment. Investors know it, which is why term sheets expire. Buyers know it, which is why discounts end at midnight. Some urgency is real, but much of it is manufactured precisely because hurried people make worse decisions — and everyone at the table knows it but you. Into this, Isaiah speaks a strange comfort: God has laid a cornerstone in Zion, a tested stone, a sure foundation, and the one who relies on it will never be stricken with panic. Notice the promise is not that the pressure disappears. It is that the person standing on the stone does not panic, because panic is what happens when everything is riding on the next move — and for you, in Christ, it is not. Your worth, your future, your name: already secured, already tested, already laid. That is what lets you ask the calm questions under a hot clock. Is this deadline real? What would I decide with one more week? Would a partner who pressures me now pressure me later? Stand on the stone. Then decide at the speed of wisdom, not the speed of fear. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, my chest is tight and the clock is loud. Remind me that nothing eternal is riding on this deadline. Give me the composure of someone standing on a foundation that was laid long before this week. Let me decide from trust, not from panic. <break time="1.1s" /> I will test whether this urgency is real before I let it set the pace of my decision. <break time="1.1s" /> Go stand on the tested stone, and let no countdown hurry your soul. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-sleep: On Sleeping On It. <break time="1.8s" /> It’s late, the document is still open, and you’re about to decide something important mostly because you’re tired of holding it. Close the laptop; morning is a means of grace. <break time="1.1s" /> “He will not let your foot slip — he who watches over you will not slumber; indeed, he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 121, verses 3 to 4. <break time="1.1s" /> Sleeping on it sounds like folk wisdom, but it is older and holier than that. The psalmist wrote for travelers on a dangerous road, with the journey still unfinished, and gave them one reason to close their eyes: the God who watches over you will not slumber. Notice the watch does not pause when yours does. That is the whole point. To sleep on a decision is to confess, with your body, that you are not the one holding the world together overnight — that God governs the hours you are unconscious just as well as the hours you are gripping the wheel. And something happens in that surrender. Morning-you is not smarter than midnight-you, but morning-you is smaller: less flooded, less cornered, less convinced that everything hangs on tonight. Fear talks loudest when you are exhausted; wisdom tends to speak at breakfast. Not every decision can wait — but far more can than midnight admits. So write down where you landed, and put it down. The One who neither slumbers nor sleeps will keep the watch you keep trying to keep yourself. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I hand You this open question for the night. Thank You that You stay awake so I don’t have to. Quiet the voice that says it must be settled tonight. Meet me in the morning with a clearer head and a steadier heart. <break time="1.1s" /> I will sleep on tonight’s decision and revisit it in the morning before I commit. <break time="1.1s" /> Go lie down and sleep, and let the God who never slumbers keep the watch until morning. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-clever: On Wisdom and Cleverness. <break time="1.8s" /> There’s a version of this decision that’s brilliant and a version that’s good, and you’ve just noticed they aren’t the same version. <break time="1.1s" /> “But the wisdom that comes from heaven is first of all pure; then peace-loving, considerate, submissive, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial and sincere.” <break time="1.1s" />James 3, verse 17. <break time="1.1s" /> Cleverness and wisdom look alike from a distance. Both are sharp; both see moves other people miss. But James gives wisdom a character reference, and it is striking what makes the list: pure, peace-loving, considerate, submissive, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, sincere. Not one word about being impressive. Cleverness finds the loophole in the contract, the phrasing that is technically true, the growth tactic that works precisely until people notice what it is. It wins quarters. Wisdom, the kind that comes from heaven, plays a longer game: it asks what the decision does to the people inside it and to the person you are becoming through it. Here is the test worth running on the choice in front of you: does this option require you to be less pure, less peaceable, less merciful, less sincere? Then it is not wisdom, however elegant the logic. This is not a tax on your ambition. It is the observation, old as Scripture, that companies compound the character of their decisions. Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, was never once merely clever. Build like Him. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I am good at finding angles, and I know it. Search this decision and show me if its brilliance is hiding a compromise. Give me the heavenly kind of wisdom — pure, peaceable, merciful, sincere. Make me the kind of builder whose smartest moves are also my most honest ones. <break time="1.1s" /> I will run this decision through the character of heavenly wisdom before I run it through the model. <break time="1.1s" /> Go be wise before you are clever, and let mercy sit in on every decision. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-ask: On Asking and Expecting. <break time="1.8s" /> You prayed about the decision — quickly, half-doubting — and went straight back to your spreadsheet. James thinks you should expect more from the asking. <break time="1.1s" /> “If any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you.” <break time="1.1s" />James 1, verse 5. <break time="1.1s" /> James makes a promise so direct it is almost uncomfortable: if any of you lacks wisdom, ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given. Not might be. Will be. Two things in that sentence should change how you pray this week. First, without finding fault: God does not roll His eyes at a founder who lacks wisdom. You will not be scolded for not knowing whether to hire the executive or kill the product line. The asking itself is welcome. Second, generously: God is not rationing clarity, doling it out to the spiritually elite. But notice what is promised — wisdom, not information. You may not receive the answer as a voice or a sign. It arrives, more often, the way wisdom always arrives: a conversation that reframes everything, a verse that will not leave you alone, a quiet settling toward one path, a flaw you suddenly see. Prayer is not a formality you perform before the real analysis. It is a request that will be answered. So ask like it. Then keep your eyes open, because something is coming back. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I lack wisdom for this decision, and I say that without shame because You hear it without fault-finding. I am asking You, specifically and expectantly, to give it. Open my eyes to recognize the answer in whatever form it takes. Thank You that You give generously, even to me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will ask God for wisdom about this decision by name and watch this week for the answer. <break time="1.1s" /> Go ask boldly, expect generously, and receive the wisdom your Father delights to give. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-d-owning: On Owning the Call. <break time="1.8s" /> You signed, you announced, and by nightfall the replay started — the other option glowing brighter now that it’s gone. This is the moment to own what you chose. <break time="1.1s" /> “In their hearts humans plan their course, but the Lord establishes their steps.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 16, verse 9. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a quiet promise buried in this proverb for the day after a decision. In their hearts humans plan their course — that was you, praying, modeling, taking counsel, choosing. But the Lord establishes their steps — and that is happening now, on the path you actually picked, not on the one you didn’t. Second-guessing feels like diligence, but it is usually something else: an attempt to keep both options alive after reality has closed one, a refusal to let the decision be finished. It splits your leadership in half. Teams can absorb a hard road; what corrodes them is a leader who is only partly here, still living in the counterfactual. Owning a decision does not mean pretending it was perfect, or that you would choose the same way with better data. It means accepting that this road, chosen in good faith, is now the terrain of God’s faithfulness. He establishes steps, not hypotheticals. So grieve the road not taken once, honestly. Then turn around, plant your feet, and lead from where you actually stand — because that is where God is establishing you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I made the call, and I keep sneaking back to relitigate it. I release the option I didn’t choose into Your hands. Establish my steps on this road, the real one, and make something good of it that I couldn’t have planned. Give me the wholeness to lead from here. <break time="1.1s" /> I will stop relitigating the decision and put my full weight behind the path I chose. <break time="1.1s" /> Go own the road you chose, and watch the Lord establish every step of it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-people: On the People Behind the Numbers. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you open the analytics today, pause and remember: every number on that screen has a name, a morning, and a life your work touches. <break time="1.1s" /> “When he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 9, verse 36. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus saw crowds the way no founder’s dashboard ever could. Where a strategist might have seen reach, market share, an audience to activate, he saw harassed and helpless people — and it moved him to compassion before it moved him to action. Your tools are built to compress people into metrics: MAUs, conversion rates, churn cohorts. The compression is useful, but it is also quietly corrosive, because you cannot love a percentage. Somewhere behind your funnel is a woman at a kitchen table trying to make your product work, a man on his lunch break filing the support ticket you skimmed. They came to you harassed by a problem, hoping you could help. The gospel insists that this is how God saw you — not as a demographic to be won but as a person to be sought, known, and carried home. Let that gaze reshape yours. Open the dashboard, yes. But before you optimize the crowd, ask Jesus to help you see it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, give me your eyes for the people I serve. Where I have flattened them into numbers, restore their faces. Move me with compassion before you move me to strategy. Thank you for seeing me as a person and not a statistic. <break time="1.1s" /> I will read one customer’s words today — a ticket, a review, an email — slowly enough to see the person who wrote them. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and look at the crowd until you see the faces — and serve them the way you have been seen. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-despise: On the Customer You’d Rather Lose. <break time="1.8s" /> There is a customer whose name you dread. Bring them with you into this quiet moment, before you answer them in any other one. <break time="1.1s" /> “Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring praise to God.” <break time="1.1s" />Romans 15, verse 7. <break time="1.1s" /> Every business has one: the customer who files the most tickets, reads the fine print aggressively, escalates everything, and pays the smallest plan while demanding the largest share of your patience. It is easy to let contempt grow in the dark — to sigh when their name appears, to answer them a little colder, to hope they churn. But Paul’s logic cuts underneath all of that: accept one another, just as Christ accepted you. You were not a low-maintenance acquisition. You came to God with endless demands, slow to trust, quick to complain, costing far more than you contributed — and he did not tolerate you; he welcomed you. That welcome is now the pattern for yours. This does not mean every customer is a fit forever, or that boundaries are unfaithful. It means that as long as they are yours, they are yours to serve without contempt. The way you speak of them when they cannot hear you is the truest measure of your service. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I confess the contempt I have nursed toward the people who are hardest to serve. Remind me how patiently you have carried me. Give me a warmth that is not performance but the overflow of being accepted by Christ. Let even my difficult customers meet kindness in me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will answer my most difficult customer this week with the same care I give my favorite one. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and welcome the one who wearies you, for so you were welcomed. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-promises: On Promises Your Product Can Keep. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere today — a sales call, a landing page, a demo — you will describe what you’ve built. Settle here first, and decide to tell the truth. <break time="1.1s" /> “All you need to say is simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’; anything beyond this comes from the evil one.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 5, verse 37. <break time="1.1s" /> The temptation rarely feels like lying. It feels like optimism: the feature is almost done, the integration mostly works, the roadmap will surely catch up to the pitch deck. You round up in the demo, soften the caveats, let the prospect believe a little more than is true — and tell yourself you are selling the vision. But Jesus asks for a simpler speech: let your yes be yes. A promise your product cannot keep is not vision; it is a debt issued in someone else’s name, and your future self, your support team, and your customer will all pay it. There is deep freedom on the other side of restraint. When your claims match your capabilities, you never have to remember what you said, never dread the onboarding call, never flinch when a customer takes you at your word. Christ, who is himself the Yes to all God’s promises, never oversold what he came to do. Sell what is real. It is enough, or it will become enough honestly. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, guard my mouth in every pitch and every promise. Take from me the fear that the truth is not enough to sell. Let my yes be yes, and let my product keep every word I say about it. I would rather grow slowly and honestly than quickly on borrowed trust. <break time="1.1s" /> I will review what we promise publicly this week and bring every claim back inside the truth. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and speak plainly of what you have made — the truth is a better salesman than the wish. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-listening: On Listening Before Building. <break time="1.8s" /> You are eager to build. Before the roadmap fills, sit still and ask whether you have actually listened to the people you’re building for. <break time="1.1s" /> “To answer before listening — that is folly and shame.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 18, verse 13. <break time="1.1s" /> A product is an answer. Every feature you ship says, in effect: this is what I heard you need. And Proverbs names the danger with uncomfortable precision — to answer before listening is folly and shame. Founders are answer-shaped people; we fall in love with solutions and then go looking for someone to have the problem. But the discipline of listening first is not just good product practice; it is a form of humility. It admits that the customer knows their own life better than your pitch deck does, that their words on a support call are worth more than your assumptions in a planning doc. God himself models this posture toward us — a Father who hears before he answers, who invites us to pour out our hearts rather than handing us prefabricated solutions. Before you write the spec, sit with five customers and mostly stay quiet. Ask what they were trying to do the last time your product frustrated them. The best roadmaps begin as good listening. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you listen to me before you answer me; teach me to do the same for the people I serve. Quiet my eagerness to be clever. Give me real curiosity about their days, their frustrations, their hopes. Let what we build next begin with what we heard. <break time="1.1s" /> I will schedule a customer conversation this week where my only job is to listen. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and hear the people you serve before you answer them in code. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-excellence: On Excellence as Love. <break time="1.8s" /> Think of the last corner you were tempted to cut. Hold it in mind, and ask who would have felt it on the other end. <break time="1.1s" /> “Do you see someone skilled in their work? They will serve before kings; they will not serve before officials of low rank.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 22, verse 29. <break time="1.1s" /> We usually justify quality in the language of business: craftsmanship builds brand, polish reduces churn, excellence commands a premium. All true, and all beside the deepest point. Excellence is a form of love. The edge case you handle gracefully is a stranger’s bad day made gentler. The error message you rewrote at midnight is a kindness to someone you will never meet. Skill, Proverbs says, carries a person into the presence of kings — but long before it impresses anyone important, it quietly serves everyone ordinary. This is how God works: a creation finished with extravagant care down to details no one would audit, pronounced good before there was a market to applaud it. Shoddiness says the user doesn’t matter enough to suffer for. Craft says the opposite. You cannot love your customers in the abstract while shipping them carelessness in the particular. So sweat the detail — not to be perfect, and not for the praise, but because a real person will live inside what you make. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, make my work an act of love and not just leverage. Give me patience for the details that only you and the end user will ever notice. Free me from perfectionism and from carelessness alike. Let the people who use what I build feel cared for. <break time="1.1s" /> I will fix one small, unglamorous thing today purely for the sake of the person who will encounter it. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and do skilled work — it is love with its sleeves rolled up. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-wrong: On Serving the Customer Who Is Wrong. <break time="1.8s" /> Someone has accused your work unfairly — a review, an email, a public thread. Before you defend yourself, sit for a moment with the One who was accused and stayed kind. <break time="1.1s" /> “When they hurled their insults at him, he did not retaliate; when he suffered, he made no threats. Instead, he entrusted himself to him who judges justly.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Peter 2, verse 23. <break time="1.1s" /> The customer is not always right. Sometimes they misread the docs, missed the email, broke it themselves, and are now angry at you in public. Everything in you wants to litigate the facts — to win. But Peter points to Jesus, who absorbed genuine injustice without retaliation, not because the facts didn’t matter but because he entrusted himself to the Judge who sees everything. That trust is what frees you here. You do not have to pretend the customer is right; honesty matters. But you can decline the fight for the last word, answer the anger with patience, and fix what you can — because your vindication is not held by a review site. It is held by God. Often the customer who is wrong is also tired, embarrassed, or afraid, and your gentleness gives them a way back without humiliation. Some of your most loyal customers will be the ones you served well on the day they least deserved it. That is, after all, your own story. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Jesus, you bore unfair words without returning them. When I am wrongly blamed, keep me from retaliation dressed up as clarification. Help me entrust my reputation to the Father and serve the person in front of me. Make my gentleness sturdier than my need to be right. <break time="1.1s" /> I will respond to the unfair complaint with patience and real help, and leave my vindication with God. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and serve even the one who wronged you — your defense is already in better hands. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-pricing: On Pricing with a Clean Conscience. <break time="1.8s" /> A price is a sentence you say to every customer before they meet you. Sit quietly and ask what yours is saying. <break time="1.1s" /> “The Lord detests dishonest scales, but accurate weights find favor with him.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 11, verse 1. <break time="1.1s" /> In the ancient market, the scale was where trust lived or died — a merchant with weighted stones could steal a little from everyone and prove it to no one. Your pricing page is your scale. And the modern temptations are subtler than shaved weights: the fee revealed only at checkout, the plan designed to be forgotten and auto-renewed, the cancellation flow built like a maze, the discount that pressures more than it serves. None of it is illegal. All of it is weighing the scale. Notice that the proverb is not merely a rule; it tells you what God loves. Accurate weights find favor with him — he delights in a business that charges what a thing is worth and says so plainly. Charging well is not the sin; your work has real value, and honest prices honor it. The sin is asymmetry: knowing something your customer doesn’t and profiting from their blindness. Price so that a fully informed customer would still shake your hand. Then the revenue that comes will rest easy on your conscience. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you detest dishonest scales — search mine. Show me anywhere my pricing profits from confusion, pressure, or forgetfulness. Give me the courage to charge fairly for real value and the integrity to make everything plain. I want revenue I never have to hide from you. <break time="1.1s" /> I will walk through my own pricing and checkout as a customer would, and make honest anything that isn’t. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and keep honest scales — let every dollar you earn be one you could explain face to face. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-followthrough: On Follow-Through After the Sale. <break time="1.8s" /> The signature is dry and the excitement has moved on to the next prospect. Come back, for a moment, to the promise you already made. <break time="1.1s" /> “…who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and does not change their mind.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 15, verse 4. <break time="1.1s" /> Every company is energetic before the sale. The demos are polished, the replies are fast, the founder himself gets on the call. The truest test comes after the money moves — when the onboarding stalls, the promised feature slips, and the customer who was courted like royalty becomes a ticket number in a queue. Psalm 15 describes the person who may dwell with God, and one mark is startlingly commercial: they keep an oath even when it hurts. Not when it’s convenient. When it hurts — when honoring the old commitment costs margin, time, and attention you would rather spend on new logos. This is covenant faithfulness scaled down to a contract, and it mirrors the God who has never once closed a deal with his people and then gone quiet. He is as attentive to you today as the day he first called you. Let your customers experience a faint echo of that: a company whose care after the invoice exceeds its charm before it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Faithful God, you keep every promise you have ever made to me, at the greatest possible cost. Make me a founder who delivers long after the deal stops being exciting. Show me the commitments I have let quietly slide. Give me joy in the unglamorous work of keeping my word. <break time="1.1s" /> I will find one promise we made before a sale that we haven’t fully kept, and keep it this week. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and keep your word when it hurts — that is where trust is actually built. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-small: On the Small Account. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere in your queue is a customer too small to matter to your revenue. Sit with the thought that they are not too small to matter. <break time="1.1s" /> “The King will reply, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.’” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 25, verse 40. <break time="1.1s" /> Sales wisdom says to tier your attention: the enterprise whale gets the dedicated Slack channel and the quarterly review; the ten-dollar-a-month customer gets the help center link. There is real prudence in focus — you cannot give everyone everything. But watch what happens in your heart when attention becomes a ranking of human worth, when the small account’s question feels like an interruption and the whale’s whim feels like a summons. Jesus stands that ranking on its head. The King, he says, hides himself in the least — the ones with nothing to offer you, no expansion revenue, no logo for your website. What you do for them, you do for him. This is not a rebuke of segmentation; it is a question about contempt. The solo freelancer on your cheapest plan trusted you with money that was not trivial to them. Serve them with the same courtesy, honesty, and follow-through you would give your largest contract. The King is watching from inside the small account. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, forgive me for measuring people by their contract value. Thank you that you did not weigh my worth before you served me. Teach me wise focus without contempt, and let the smallest customer we have be treated with dignity. Help me see you in the least of these. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give one small customer this week the level of care we reserve for our biggest. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and serve the least as though serving the King — because you are. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-c-grateful: On Gratitude for Your Customers. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you check today’s revenue, stop and marvel at the stranger arithmetic underneath it: real people chose to pay for something you made. <break time="1.1s" /> “I thank my God every time I remember you. In all my prayers for all of you, I always pray with joy because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now.” <break time="1.1s" />Philippians 1, verses 3 to 5. <break time="1.1s" /> Paul had financial supporters, and look how he thought of them: not as a donor base to be retained, but as partners he thanked God for by name, with joy, every time they crossed his mind. Somewhere along the way a founder’s gratitude tends to invert. Early on, the first paying customer felt like a miracle — you remember exactly who it was. A few hundred invoices later, payment feels like what customers owe you, and your attention goes only to the ones who leave. But every renewal is a quiet, renewed act of trust: a person deciding, again, that what you made is worth their limited money. None of it was owed to you. Behind their choice stands the God who supplies every customer you have ever had — the market is not your creation any more than the harvest belongs to the farmer alone. Gratitude re-humanizes the ledger. Thank God for your customers by name, and some of Paul’s joy will find its way into your work. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, thank you for every person who has ever paid for what we made. I confess I have treated their trust as routine. Give me Paul’s habit of remembering people with joy before you. Let gratitude, not entitlement, set the tone of this company. <break time="1.1s" /> I will thank God today for three customers by name, and send one of them a genuine note of thanks. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into this day grateful — every customer you have is a gift you did not create. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-table:
On Being at the Table. <break time="1.8s" /> You can sit at the dinner table and still be somewhere else entirely. Tonight, come all the way home. <break time="1.1s" /> “You will eat the fruit of your labor; blessings and prosperity will be yours. Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 128, verses 2 to 3. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice where this psalm puts the blessing of work. Not in the field where the labor happened, not in the barn where the harvest is counted, but at a table, surrounded by faces. The fruit of your labor is meant to be eaten in company. That was always the point of the field.

Founders are good at deferral. We tell ourselves the table will get our full attention after the raise, after the launch, after the fire is out. But there is always another fire, and meanwhile the olive shoots around your table are growing whether you are watching or not. The psalmist does not scold the worker for working; he simply insists that the work bends toward the table, not the other way around.

The gospel makes this possible, because in Christ your worth is already settled — you do not have to keep earning it after hours. The One who fed five thousand and then sat down to eat with his friends invites you to do the smaller, harder thing: put the phone in another room, look up, and taste the fruit you have been too busy to enjoy. The blessing is not the harvest. It is the meal. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, thank you for the people around my table, who are a greater blessing than anything I am building. Forgive me for being present in body and absent in mind. Quiet the part of me that keeps working after the work is done. Teach me to receive the meal you have set before me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will eat one meal today with no screen in reach and my full attention on the people in front of me. <break time="1.1s" /> Go home all the way, and taste the fruit of your labor with the people it was for. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-spouse:
On the One Who Married You. <break time="1.8s" /> Your spouse did not marry the company. They married you — and lately they may be getting whatever is left over. <break time="1.1s" /> “‘…and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” <break time="1.1s" />Mark 10, verses 8 to 9. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus says two things about marriage here, and both cut close for a founder. First, that it is a joining — two lives made one flesh, a union deeper than any operating agreement. Second, that things will try to separate it. He says “let no one separate,” and we usually imagine a rival. But the thing prying a founder’s marriage apart is rarely a person. It is a company: a demanding, fascinating, always-hungry third party that follows you to bed on a glowing screen.

Here is the uncomfortable arithmetic. Your spouse made vows to you; your company did not. Your spouse will be there if the company dies; the company will not return the favor. Yet it is astonishingly easy to give the company your best hours, your best thinking, your best patience — and hand your marriage the exhausted remainder.

Christ loves his church not with leftovers but with his whole self, and that love is both the model and the fuel. You cannot pour out what you have not received. So receive it, and then go home and give your first fruits — attention, tenderness, time — to the one who actually said yes to you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you joined us together, and I confess I have let the company push its way between us. Forgive me for giving my best to the business and my leftovers to my beloved. Fill me with your love so I have something real to bring home. Guard what you have joined. <break time="1.1s" /> I will plan one unhurried evening with my spouse this week and protect it like an investor meeting. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and give your first and best to the one who vowed to share your life. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-kids:
On What Your Children See. <break time="1.8s" /> Your children will never read the cap table. But they are reading your face, every single day. <break time="1.1s" /> “These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.” <break time="1.1s" />Deuteronomy 6, verses 6 to 7. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice how ordinary the classroom is. Moses does not tell parents to schedule formal instruction; he points to sitting at home, walking down the road, lying down, getting up. The faith is passed along in the margins — the unguarded, in-between moments when a child watches how you actually live.

Which is sobering for a founder, because your children are studying you in exactly those moments. They see the face you make when you check your phone at breakfast. They hear the tone you use after a hard board call. Long before they understand what you do, they understand what it does to you. You are impressing something on them in every ordinary hour; the only question is what.

Here is the grace in it: the same ordinariness that convicts you also frees you. You do not need to engineer perfect moments or compensate with grand gestures. You need only be there — at the table, on the road, at bedtime — with a heart where God’s words actually live. Children do not need an impressive parent. They need a present one, whose face tells them the truth: that they matter more than anything you are building. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, my children are watching me more closely than any investor ever will. Let them see on my face that they are loved, not that they are an interruption. Write your words on my heart so that what spills out in ordinary moments is worth catching. Make me a present parent before a successful founder. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give my children my undivided face at one ordinary moment today — a meal, a drive, a bedtime — with nothing else in my hands. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and let your children read, in your face, how much they are loved. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-friends:
On Friendship Without an Agenda. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere along the way, every coffee became a meeting. You may have contacts everywhere and friends nowhere. <break time="1.1s" /> “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for a time of adversity.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 17, verse 17. <break time="1.1s" /> The proverb measures friendship by one test: does the love hold at all times? Not when it is strategic, not when you are useful, not while your star is rising — at all times, and especially in adversity. A friend is the person who shows up when there is nothing in it for them.

Founding a company quietly corrodes this. Your calendar fills with relationships that are really transactions wearing friendship’s clothes. Everyone wants something; soon you assume everyone does, and — more quietly — you start approaching people the same way, sorting every room by usefulness. It is a lonely way to live, and the loneliness compounds like debt.

Jesus called his disciples friends — not assets, not a network, friends — and he proved it in adversity, loving them at the precise moment they were most useless to him. That is the friendship you already have, and it is the kind you are freed to give. So keep the friend who knew you before the company, who is bored by your metrics and interested in your soul. Answer their call. Waste an evening with them. Nothing is wasted that teaches you to love at all times. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord Jesus, you called your disciples friends and loved them when they brought you nothing. Forgive me for sorting people by their usefulness. Give me one or two friendships with no agenda, and make me the kind of friend who loves at all times. Teach me to waste time well. <break time="1.1s" /> I will reach out to one friend today with no ask, no update, and no agenda — just to be a friend. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and love someone at all times, expecting nothing back. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-body:
On the Body You Build With. <break time="1.8s" /> You steward the company’s runway carefully. Your body has a runway too, and you have been spending it like it is infinite. <break time="1.1s" /> “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore honor God with your bodies.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Corinthians 6, verses 19 to 20. <break time="1.1s" /> Founders talk about their bodies the way they talk about servers: something to be pushed to capacity, patched with caffeine, rebooted on weekends if the roadmap allows. The four hours of sleep become a badge. The skipped meals, the vanished workouts, the strange chest-tightness you have decided not to mention — all filed under the cost of building.

Paul will not let you file it there. Your body is not company property; it is not even your property. It is a temple — a dwelling place of God, bought at the price of Christ’s own body. “You are not your own” cuts two ways: it humbles you, and it dignifies the flesh and bone you have been treating as expendable. You would never let a team member run a sacred site into the ground. You are running one.

This is not a call to vanity or optimization; it is a call to stewardship. Sleep is not weakness — it is trust, a nightly confession that God runs the world without you. Eat like a person who expects to be here for the long game. The company needs a founder, and your people need you, alive and whole. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you knit this body together and bought it at a price, and I have treated it like a machine that owes me output. Forgive my proud exhaustion. Teach me to sleep as an act of trust and to care for my health as an act of worship. Keep me whole for the long work you have given me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will choose one concrete act of bodily stewardship today — a full night’s sleep, a real meal, or a walk — and treat it as obedience, not indulgence. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and honor God with the body he bought, resting like someone who trusts him. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-home:
On What You Carry Through the Door. <break time="1.8s" /> The workday ends, but the weight does not. Before you walk through your front door tonight, there is somewhere else to set it down. <break time="1.1s" /> “Cast your cares on the Lord and he will sustain you; he will never let the righteous be shaken.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 55, verse 22. <break time="1.1s" /> Anxiety does not respect commutes. You can leave the office, close the laptop, silence the notifications — and still carry the payroll worry, the difficult conversation, the slipping deadline straight into your kitchen. Your family feels it before you say a word. Stress leaks: into shortened answers, distracted eyes, a tension in the house that children notice and cannot name.

The psalmist offers a different destination for the weight. Cast it — an active, physical word, like heaving a load off your shoulders — on the Lord. Not on your spouse, who becomes an unpaid therapist. Not on your kids, who learn to tiptoe. On God, and with one staggering promise: he will sustain you. Not your metrics. You.

The founder’s instinct is to carry everything, because carrying things is the job. But your family did not sign up to live under your load, and God never asked you to bring it home. Some founders find it helps to make the casting literal: a prayer at a stoplight, a pause on the porch, naming each worry and handing it over before the door opens. What you set down there, you do not put on the people you love. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you see everything I am carrying tonight, and you invite me to throw it onto your shoulders. Forgive me for making my family live under a weight you offered to take. I name my worries now and hand them to you, one by one. Let me walk through my door lighter than I left work. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pause before walking in the door tonight and name each work worry to God before I greet the people I love. <break time="1.1s" /> Cast the whole weight on the One who sustains you, and walk through your door unburdened. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-realyou:
On Being Fully Known. <break time="1.8s" /> You have gotten very good at presenting yourself. But nobody can love a pitch deck — and the polished you is starting to feel lonely. <break time="1.1s" /> “You have searched me, Lord, and you know me. You know when I sit and when I rise; you perceive my thoughts from afar.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 139, verses 1 to 2. <break time="1.1s" /> Founders live in permanent presentation mode. Every conversation is a little pitch: confident to investors, steady to employees, fine — always fine — to friends and family. Over time the performance stops being something you do and starts being somewhere you live. And it is airless in there, because a curated self can be admired but never loved. Love requires access to the real thing.

The psalmist has stopped performing. “You have searched me, Lord, and you know me.” God knows when you sit and when you rise — the version of you that slumps at midnight, doubts the whole enterprise, checks the numbers again out of fear. He perceives the thoughts you would never say on a podcast. And the astonishment of the gospel is that this total exposure meets total love: fully known and fully kept, at the cross, at the same time.

That security is what makes honesty with people possible. You do not have to be flawless to be loved, because the One who knows you completely has not left. So let someone in past the deck — a spouse, a friend, a pastor. Tell them one true thing you have been managing. Being known is the only cure for being alone. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you have searched me and known me, and you love me still. Forgive me for performing even with the people closest to me. Give me the courage to be honest with someone this week about how things really are. Let your perfect knowledge of me make me brave. <break time="1.1s" /> I will tell one trusted person the unpolished truth about how I am actually doing. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and let yourself be known, for the One who knows you fully loves you completely. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-without:
On Who You Are Without It. <break time="1.8s" /> Try to finish this sentence without mentioning the company: “I am…” If you can’t, today is for you. <break time="1.1s" /> “See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are!” <break time="1.1s" />1 John 3, verse 1. <break time="1.1s" /> At some point the company stopped being what you do and became who you are. It is an easy trade to make. The business carries your name or your fingerprints; its wins feel like your worth and its losses like your judgment. Ask yourself what happens inside when someone asks, “So what do you do?” — and imagine answering after the company has failed, or sold, or simply moved on without you. If the answer is vertigo, the company is holding something it was never built to hold.

John hands you a sturdier identity, and he can hardly contain himself doing it: “See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are!” Not called founders, CEOs, or operators — children. It is not a title you earned, so it is not a title you can lose. No down round can dilute it; no acquirer can take it off the table.

This does not make the company matter less. It makes the company safe to hold, because it is no longer load-bearing. You can build with open hands when your name is already secure — lavished on you, before you ever shipped a thing. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I confess that I have let the company answer the question only you can answer. Thank you for lavishing your love on me and calling me your child before I built anything. Loosen my grip on this identity I have manufactured. Let me build from belovedness, not for it. <break time="1.1s" /> I will write down who I am in five sentences that never mention the company, and keep the list where I can see it. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into your work as a child of God first, and a founder a distant second. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-celebrate:
On Celebrating at Home. <break time="1.8s" /> The team got the champagne. The Slack channel got the emoji storm. Did your family get anything but the tired version of you? <break time="1.1s" /> “There, in the presence of the Lord your God, you and your families shall eat and shall rejoice in everything you have put your hand to, because the Lord your God has blessed you.” <break time="1.1s" />Deuteronomy 12, verse 7. <break time="1.1s" /> When God taught Israel to celebrate, he specified the guest list. Rejoicing in “everything you have put your hand to” was not to happen in a boardroom of colleagues — it was to happen with your family, in the presence of God, around food. The people who share your ordinary life were meant to share your joy.

Founders often get this exactly backwards. The victories are celebrated at work, with the people who understand the metrics, while home gets the exhaust: the stress, the late nights, the distracted silences. Your family absorbs the costs of the company but is somehow never invited to its joys. Over time they learn that the business only takes from them — because from where they sit, it only does.

Notice, too, why Israel could rejoice: “because the Lord your God has blessed you.” Celebration is theology. Bringing a win home and telling the story at your own table is a way of confessing that the blessing came from God and belongs to the whole household that sacrificed for it. So next time something good happens, do not just toast the team. Buy the ice cream. Tell your kids why tonight is special. Let the people who paid for the win taste it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, every good thing in this company came from your hand. Forgive me for celebrating with colleagues and bringing only fatigue home to my family. Teach me to rejoice in your presence with the people who sacrifice the most for this work. Make our table a place where your blessings get named. <break time="1.1s" /> I will bring the next win home — telling the story at our table and celebrating with my family, however small the occasion. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and rejoice before the Lord with your family in everything you have put your hand to. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-b-longview:
On a Life Well Spent. <break time="1.8s" /> One day the building will be over, and you will look back on how you spent it all. What do you want to be true then? <break time="1.1s" /> “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” <break time="1.1s" />2 Timothy 4, verse 7. <break time="1.1s" /> Paul writes this from a prison cell, near the end, doing what every builder eventually does: looking back over a whole life and asking what it amounted to. His summary is striking for what it leaves out. No metrics. No headcount of churches planted or letters written. Just three things: I fought the good fight, I finished the race, I kept the faith.

Founders are trained to think in quarters and rounds, but a life is graded on the whole arc. And from the far end, the ledger reads differently. No one at the finish line says, “I wish I had answered more email.” The questions that survive are Paul’s kind: Did I fight for things worth fighting for? Did I finish what I was actually given to run — not just the company, but the marriage, the children, the friendships, the faith? Did I keep the one thing that could not be replaced?

Here is the mercy: the race Paul finished was not a performance for God’s approval but a response to it — grace at the starting line, not just the tape. You are free to run the long race today, in small choices: the dinner kept, the Sabbath taken, the friend called. A life well spent is simply many days spent well. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, teach me to see my days from the finish line. I do not want to win the quarter and lose the life you gave me. Show me what fighting the good fight means this week — in my home, my friendships, and my work. Keep me faithful in the small daily choices that become a whole life. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name the races I am actually running — faith, family, friendship, work — and make one choice today that serves the whole arc, not just the quarter. <break time="1.1s" /> Run today so that, at the end, you can say you fought well, finished, and kept the faith. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-now: On Joy That Doesn’t Wait for the Exit. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you check a single metric, ask yourself an honest question: when, exactly, did you decide joy would have to wait? <break time="1.1s" /> “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!” <break time="1.1s" />Philippians 4, verse 4. <break time="1.1s" /> Paul did not write “Rejoice in the Lord always” from a corner office after a good quarter. He wrote it from a prison cell, to a church he could not visit, about a future he could not see. Founders are fluent in deferred joy: I will be happy after the raise closes, after we hit profitability, after the exit. But “after” is a horizon, and horizons recede as you walk toward them. Whatever milestone you reach, another will take its place, still promising the happiness the last one owed you. Paul’s word is “always” — which includes today, with its unfinished roadmap and its unproven model. That is only possible because the joy is in the Lord, not in the circumstances. What Christ has secured for you — forgiveness, adoption, a future no term sheet can touch — is already fully vested. Nothing on your cap table can add to it, and no down round can dilute it. You do not have to wait for the exit to rejoice. The best reason you will ever have, you have now. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I confess I have treated joy like a bonus that pays out at the end. Teach me to rejoice in you today, in the unfinished middle of this work. Untangle my gladness from my milestones and anchor it in what you have already secured. Let me build from joy instead of toward it. <break time="1.1s" /> I will rejoice today, in the middle of the work, because my deepest reasons for joy are already secure in Christ. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and be glad now — the joy of the Lord is not waiting on your exit. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-thanks: On Thanking the People Who Built It With You. <break time="1.8s" /> Sit quietly and let the faces come to mind — the ones who believed early, stayed late, and asked for nothing. Hold them there for a moment. <break time="1.1s" /> “We always thank God for all of you and continually mention you in our prayers. We remember before our God and Father your work produced by faith, your labor prompted by love, and your endurance inspired by hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Thessalonians 1, verses 2 to 3. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice how Paul begins his letter: not with strategy, not with correction, but with thanks — “we always thank God for all of you.” He remembered the Thessalonians’ work produced by faith, their labor prompted by love, their endurance — and he made sure they heard it. Somewhere in your company are people like that: the ones who took the pay cut, stayed the late night, believed before the evidence came in. It is easy for a founder to absorb their work into the word “we” and move on to the next fire. But gratitude that stays unspoken slowly reads as absence, and people can labor a long time on very little except the hope that someone noticed. You did not build this alone. The engineer who rewrote the billing system, the first customer who took a chance, the spouse who carried the household through the lean year — these are graces with faces. The gospel makes thanking them easy, because you have nothing you did not receive; even your grit was given. So say it plainly and by name. Thank-you is not a soft skill. It is the sound a heart makes when it finally tells the truth about how anything gets built. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, thank you for every person who has carried this work with me. Forgive me for the gratitude I have felt but never said. Bring to my mind today the names that most need to hear it, and give me words that are specific and true. Let the people who built this with me know they are seen. <break time="1.1s" /> I will thank one person today, by name and in detail, for something they built with me. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and say the thank-you out loud — unspoken gratitude helps no one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-ordinary: On Ordinary Graces. <break time="1.8s" /> Slow down before the day blurs past. Some of what God is giving you today will be small enough to miss. <break time="1.1s" /> “I know that there is nothing better for people than to be happy and to do good while they live. That each of them may eat and drink, and find satisfaction in all their toil — this is the gift of God.” <break time="1.1s" />Ecclesiastes 3, verses 12 to 13. <break time="1.1s" /> Ecclesiastes is a hard-eyed book, written by someone who chased every large thing — wealth, projects, reputation — and watched them evaporate like mist. His conclusion is startlingly small: eat, drink, find satisfaction in your toil, for this is the gift of God. Not the exit; the lunch. Not the legacy; the good hour of work. A founder’s eyes are trained on the distant and the enormous, which makes the near and the small invisible: the first coffee while the office is still quiet, a colleague solving something elegantly, sunlight on the desk at four o’clock, a customer’s offhand thank-you. These are not filler between the moments that matter. They are the daily bread of joy, given by a Father who knew you would need feeding far more often than you would need triumphs. Grace rarely announces itself; it sets the table and waits to be noticed. Today, notice. The gift of God is already scattered through your workday, hidden in plain sight, patient as bread. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, open my eyes to the ordinary graces I walk past every day. Thank you for food and light and good work and the people beside me in it. Teach me to find satisfaction in my toil as a gift from your hand. Make me a person who notices. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pause three times today to name one small, ordinary gift sitting in plain sight. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and receive the small gifts of this day — they were set out for you on purpose. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-otherswin: On Celebrating Someone Else’s Win. <break time="1.8s" /> Think of the announcement that stung a little — the round, the acquisition, the milestone that wasn’t yours. Bring that exact feeling here. <break time="1.1s" /> “Rejoice with those who rejoice; mourn with those who mourn.” <break time="1.1s" />Romans 12, verse 15. <break time="1.1s" /> Of the two commands in this verse, founders usually find the second easier. Mourning with a struggling peer costs sympathy; rejoicing with a winning one costs something dearer — the story that you are ahead. When a competitor announces the round you wanted, or a friend sells the company while you are still grinding, envy arrives before you have chosen it. It whispers that the market is zero-sum and so is worth. But the gospel un-ranks you. Your standing before God was never relative; Christ did not die for your percentile. He died for you, and what he secured cannot be outraised or acquired out from under you. That is what makes genuine celebration possible: their win takes nothing from you, because nothing that matters about you was ever up for comparison. So send the message. Make it warm and specific, and resist the urge to mention your own progress in the same breath. You will find, strangely, that celebrating someone else’s win is a door out of the small room of self, and joy is waiting on the other side. Envy shrinks the world to a ladder. Rejoicing opens it back into a field. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you know the envy I dress up as ambition. Free me from measuring my worth against other people’s announcements. Give me a heart that can be genuinely glad when someone else wins, because my standing with you was settled at the cross. Make my congratulations honest. <break time="1.1s" /> I will send a genuine, specific congratulation today to someone whose success I have quietly envied. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and rejoice with those who rejoice — their win was never your loss. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-record: On Writing Down What Went Right. <break time="1.8s" /> Your memory keeps meticulous records of failure and loses the receipts for grace. Come ready to correct the books. <break time="1.1s" /> “Praise the Lord, my soul, and forget not all his benefits.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 103, verse 2. <break time="1.1s" /> The psalmist commands his own soul to remember, which tells you something: forgetting is the default. Nobody has to be told to remember the churned customer, the failed launch, the investor who passed. Wounds keep their own records. Benefits do not — they slip quietly out of memory unless someone writes them down. This is why gratitude, for a founder, has to become a discipline rather than a mood: a few lines at the end of the day naming what went right. The deal that closed. The bug that didn’t ship. The colleague who covered for you. The provision that arrived, again, on time. Israel stacked stones beside rivers so their children would ask what happened here; your notebook can be a stack of stones. On the bad days — and they will come — you will open it and find the evidence your feelings have misplaced: that God has been faithful in this venture, specifically, repeatedly, in ink. Praise the Lord, my soul, and forget not. Memory is where gratitude lives, and memory needs help. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, my soul forgets your benefits with astonishing speed. Give me the small discipline of writing down what went right, and the honesty to see how much of it was you. Build me a record I can return to on the days when my feelings lie. Teach my soul to remember. <break time="1.1s" /> I will write down three things that went right today before I close my laptop. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and keep the record of God’s benefits — you will need it sooner than you think. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-craft: On Delight in the Craft Itself. <break time="1.8s" /> Remember the thing you actually love doing — the part of the work you would do even if no one paid you. Start there. <break time="1.1s" /> “…and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, with understanding, with knowledge and with all kinds of skills — to make artistic designs for work in gold, silver and bronze, to cut and set stones, to work in wood, and to engage in all kinds of crafts.” <break time="1.1s" />Exodus 31, verses 3 to 5. <break time="1.1s" /> The first person Scripture describes as filled with the Spirit of God is not a prophet or a king. He is a craftsman — Bezalel, named and gifted for work in gold and stone and wood. Before the Spirit ever wrote through poets, he steadied the hands of a maker. That should recalibrate how you see the work itself. Somewhere under the fundraising and the forecasting is the thing you actually love doing — the clean line of code, the sentence that finally says it, the product decision that clicks into place like a well-cut joint. It is easy to treat that delight as a luxury the business can no longer afford, a hobby the CEO version of you was supposed to outgrow. But delight in craft is not a distraction from your calling; it is part of the image of God in you — the Maker’s likeness enjoying making. So return to the workbench sometimes for no strategic reason at all. Do one thing today slowly and well, for the sheer goodness of doing it. The Spirit who filled Bezalel is not embarrassed by your joy in the work. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, thank you for making me a maker. Forgive me for treating the craft I love as an inefficiency to be delegated away. Restore my delight in doing one thing slowly and well, and let that delight be worship. Fill my hands the way you filled Bezalel’s. <break time="1.1s" /> I will spend one unhurried hour this week on the part of the craft I love, for its own sake. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and make something well today — the Maker delights in your delight. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-laughter: On Laughter in the Office. <break time="1.8s" /> Ask yourself when you last heard real laughter at work — and what its absence might be telling you. <break time="1.1s" /> “Our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with songs of joy. Then it was said among the nations, ‘The Lord has done great things for them.’ The Lord has done great things for us, and we are filled with joy.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 126, verses 2 to 3. <break time="1.1s" /> When God restored the fortunes of Zion, the evidence was audible: mouths filled with laughter, and the watching nations drawing their conclusion — the Lord has done great things for them. The laughter was the testimony. It is worth asking, then, what your office sounds like. Startups run on urgency, and urgency left unmanaged curdles into grimness: meetings without a single smile, channels stripped of play, a culture where seriousness is mistaken for commitment. But grimness is not a strategy; it is a leak. Teams that never laugh together are storing up a tension that will eventually spend itself somewhere worse. Laughter is not the opposite of hard work. It is the sound of people who believe, somewhere beneath the metrics, that they are safe — that failure here will not be fatal, that the Lord has done great things and may yet do more. As the founder, you set the license. If you can laugh, they can. So let something be funny today. Tell the story of your worst demo. Joy shared aloud is a load lifted, and a witness besides. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, thank you for laughter and for the great things you have done for us. Loosen the grimness I have modeled and mistaken for diligence. Make our office a place where people are safe enough to laugh. Fill my own mouth first. <break time="1.1s" /> I will bring lightness into one meeting today and let my team see me laugh. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and let laughter be heard in your halls — it tells the truth about what God has done. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-wonder: On Keeping Wonder Alive. <break time="1.8s" /> Try to see your company the way you saw it in the first month — before familiarity filed down the astonishment. <break time="1.1s" /> “Great are the works of the Lord; they are pondered by all who delight in them.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 111, verse 2. <break time="1.1s" /> “Pondered by all who delight in them” — the psalmist assumes that delight and attention feed each other. You delight, so you look closer; you look closer, and the delight deepens. Every founder knows the honeymoon phase, when the whole enterprise was astonishing: the first user you didn’t know personally, the first invoice, the login screen with your own logo on it. Then repetition did what repetition does, and the miraculous became infrastructure. But familiarity is not truth; it is only anesthesia. The thing you built is still improbable. Strangers still trust you with their money and their hours. People still gather every morning to make something exist that didn’t. The works of the Lord are great, and your company — sustained, provided for, held together through everything that should have ended it — is one of the places his works can be pondered. Wonder, after the honeymoon, is not a feeling you wait for but an attention you practice. Slow down long enough today to actually see the thing. Delight is downstream of looking, and there is more here than you have stopped noticing. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, familiarity has dulled my eyes to what you have done here. Give me back the astonishment I had at the beginning, not as nostalgia but as clear sight. Teach me to ponder your works in the middle of my own company. Keep wonder alive in me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will stop today and deliberately marvel at one thing about this company that I have started taking for granted. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and look closely at what God has built through you — wonder belongs to those who keep looking. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-badnumbers: On Gratitude When the Numbers Are Bad. <break time="1.8s" /> You don’t have to pretend the numbers are good to come to God grateful. Come with the red dashboard in hand. <break time="1.1s" /> “…give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Thessalonians 5, verse 18. <break time="1.1s" /> Paul does not say give thanks for all circumstances, as though a cratering quarter were itself a gift. He says give thanks in them — inside the bad month, standing in it, without pretending it is anything other than it is. That distinction rescues gratitude from dishonesty. When the dashboard is red, you are not asked to call it green. You are asked to look past the dashboard to what remains true regardless: provision that has carried you this far, people still at their desks, a Savior whose claim on you does not fluctuate with revenue. “In Christ Jesus” is the anchor of the sentence — circumstances change weekly; your position in him does not. Bad numbers are loud, and they will gladly narrate your whole life if you let them: everything is failing, nothing has worked, you are your churn rate. Thanksgiving is how you take the microphone back. It does not fix the quarter. It fixes the accounting — reminding you that the truest ledger was settled at the cross, and it shows you rich.
