Give thanks in it. Then get back to work, lighter. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, the numbers are not what I hoped, and I won’t pretend otherwise. Even here, thank you — for provision, for the people still beside me, for a standing in Christ that no quarter can touch. Quiet the voice that says the dashboard is the whole story. Teach me thanksgiving with my eyes open. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name five true reasons for gratitude today that no bad metric can erase. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and give thanks inside the hard season — your riches in Christ do not fluctuate. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-j-resistance: On Joy as Resistance. <break time="1.8s" /> Notice the protective crust of irony you’ve grown — the reflex to expect the worst so nothing can disappoint you. Set it down for these few minutes. <break time="1.1s" /> “This day is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the Lord is your strength.” <break time="1.1s" />Nehemiah 8, verse 10. <break time="1.1s" /> The wall was finished but the city was still fragile, and when the Law was read aloud the people wept at how far they had fallen. Nehemiah’s response is startling: stop grieving, eat well, share the feast — the joy of the Lord is your strength. Not your reward after strength; your strength itself. Founders marinate in reasons for cynicism. Enough broken promises, ghosted deals, and pivots that were really funerals, and irony starts to feel like intelligence: expect nothing and you can never be played. But cynicism is not protection; it is pre-emptive surrender, grief wearing armor. Joy is the resistance. To be glad — deliberately, publicly, in a world that keeps handing you reasons not to be — is to insist that God’s goodness is a harder fact than the market’s indifference. This is not naivety; the joyful person has usually seen everything the cynic has seen and refused the conclusion. Christ has risen, and the ending of the story is not in doubt. So celebrate on purpose. Every feast you keep is a small act of defiance against despair, and despair deserves to lose. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, cynicism has been quietly recruiting me, and I have half let it. Forgive me for calling my guardedness wisdom. Give me the defiant joy of people who know how the story ends, and make that joy my strength. Let my gladness be a protest against despair. <break time="1.1s" /> I will choose one deliberate act of celebration this week as a quiet refusal of cynicism. <break time="1.1s" /> Go in defiant gladness — the joy of the Lord is your strength, and despair has already lost. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-pr-first: On Praying Before the Calendar Takes Over. <break time="1.8s" /> The calendar has not claimed this moment yet. Before the first notification arrives, give the first minutes to the One who gives you the day. <break time="1.1s" /> “Very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, left the house and went off to a solitary place, where he prayed.” <break time="1.1s" />Mark 1, verse 35. <break time="1.1s" /> Mark notices the timing: very early, while it was still dark. Jesus had every reason to sleep in — the previous evening the whole town had gathered at his door, and more would gather today. Demand was not going to let up. So he got up before it did. Notice that he did not pray because the day was empty; he prayed because it was full. Your calendar will begin making claims on you the moment you look at it, and those claims are not neutral — they will tell you what matters, what is urgent, who you are. The first voice you listen to tends to run the day. This is not a summons to heroic discipline so much as an invitation to honesty: you cannot pour out what you have not received. Jesus withdrew to be with his Father because that was where his life came from — and then he went back to the crowds. The order matters. Grace first, then work. Receive the day before you attempt to run it, and the running changes. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, before the day tells me who I am, let me hear it from you. Meet me in these first quiet minutes the way you met your Son in the dark. Give me what I will need to pour out, because I cannot manufacture it myself. Then send me into the crowds with your voice still in my ears. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give God the first minutes of the day before the calendar takes the rest. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into your full day having first been filled, and let the earliest voice you heard be the one that runs it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-pr-meeting: On the First Meeting of the Day. <break time="1.8s" /> You keep the meetings you believe matter. Come now to the one standing meeting whose other party never cancels. <break time="1.1s" /> “In the morning, LORD, you hear my voice; in the morning I lay my requests before you and wait expectantly.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 5, verse 3. <break time="1.1s" /> David describes prayer the way you might describe a standing meeting. There is an agenda — requests, laid out plainly. There is a stakeholder — the LORD, who hears. And there is follow-up — waiting, expectantly, to see what he will do. Founders keep the meetings they believe matter. You would never skip a session with your lead investor because the week got busy; you would move other things. So the question is not really whether you have time to pray, but whose meeting you believe it is. Here is the wonder the psalm simply assumes: the God who runs the universe takes this meeting. Every morning. He hears your voice — not a summary, not a delegate, your voice. You did not earn the slot with performance; it was purchased for you, and the door stays open. So put it first on the calendar. Name your requests like line items, hold nothing back for polish, and then do the strangest part: wait expectantly, like someone who believes the other party actually showed up. He did. He does. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you hear my voice this morning, and I hardly know what to do with that. I lay my requests before you plainly — the deal, the hire, the fear I have told no one. Teach me to treat this meeting as the one the whole day depends on. And teach me to wait for you expectantly, not anxiously. <break time="1.1s" /> I will take my meeting with God first, and bring him my real agenda. <break time="1.1s" /> Walk into every other meeting today carrying the quiet of the first one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-pr-competitors: On Praying for Your Competitors. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere this morning, your competitor is also drinking coffee, also worried, also hoping. Bring them with you into prayer. <break time="1.1s" /> “But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 5, verse 44. <break time="1.1s" /> Your competitors are probably not your persecutors. But they are the nearest thing the market gives you to an enemy — the company whose funding announcement tightens your chest, whose customer wins feel like personal losses. Jesus’ instruction reaches even that far: pray for them. Not against them, not about them — for them. Try it and you will discover why he commanded it. It is nearly impossible to envy someone you are sincerely asking God to bless. Prayer does its surgery on the one praying; it pries loose the quiet belief that their success is your failure, that the world runs on scarcity and God distributes in zero-sum. He does not. The Father who feeds sparrows and clothes lilies is not running out of provision, and their win does not shrink his supply toward you. You can ask for their team to flourish, their families to be well, their work to serve customers honestly — and still build hard to win yours. What you cannot do is resent them and stay soft toward God. Pray for them by name. It will change less about them than it changes in you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I bring you the people I compete against, by name, and I ask you to bless them. Forgive me for the times I have quietly wished them harm and called it strategy. Uproot my belief in scarcity and replace it with trust in your provision. Make me a founder who can build hard and love freely at the same time. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pray for my competitors by name, asking God to bless what I am tempted to envy. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and compete today with open hands, blessing the very ones you are running against. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-pr-through: On Praying Through a Decision. <break time="1.8s" /> Bring the decision here while it is still open — not for a signature, but for company. Let the question sit between you and God for a while. <break time="1.1s" /> “One of those days Jesus went out to a mountainside to pray, and spent the night praying to God. When morning came, he called his disciples to him and chose twelve of them, whom he also designated apostles.” <break time="1.1s" />Luke 6, verses 12 to 13. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice the order of events. First the mountainside, then the whole night of prayer, and only when morning came did Jesus choose the twelve. He did not draft the list and then ask his Father to sign off on it. The praying came before the deciding, and shaped it. Most of us do it the other way around. We analyze, we model, we make up our minds — and then we ask God to bless the decision, prayer as a rubber stamp on a done deal. Praying through a decision is different. It means bringing the open question into God’s presence while it is still open: naming the options, confessing what you are afraid of, admitting which outcome you secretly want, and staying long enough for your desires to be rearranged. You may not hear a verdict. Often you will simply find the fog has thinned and one path has grown quietly plausible. But even when the answer stays hidden, something else happens: the decision stops being a weight you carry alone. You choose in company. That was the point all along. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, here is the decision, still open, and here is my heart, not neutral. I confess the outcome I secretly want and the outcome I fear. Rearrange my desires until they can be trusted, and thin the fog enough for a next step. And whether or not you show me the answer, keep me company in the choosing. <break time="1.1s" /> I will bring my next big decision to God while it is still open, not after I have made it. <break time="1.1s" /> Decide nothing alone today — carry the open question up the mountainside first. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-pr-short: On Prayers Between Meetings. <break time="1.8s" /> You have thirty seconds before the next thing. That is enough. God has never once required a quiet hour before he would listen. <break time="1.1s" /> “The king said to me, ‘What is it you want?’ Then I prayed to the God of heaven, and I answered the king.” <break time="1.1s" />Nehemiah 2, verses 4 to 5. <break time="1.1s" /> Nehemiah’s prayer happens in the space between a question and an answer. The king asks what he wants; the next words out of his mouth will shape everything; and in that sliver of a moment — “Then I prayed to the God of heaven” — he prays. No closed door, no bowed head, no time. A breath, aimed upward, in the middle of the highest-stakes meeting of his life. Scripture does not apologize for the brevity. It records it as prayer, full stop. This matters for founders whose days are a corridor of back-to-back meetings. You will not always get the quiet hour, and on many days the only prayers you manage will be thirty seconds in a stairwell, a sentence before you join the call, a help me under your breath. Those count. Not because God grades on a curve, but because he is a Father, and fathers hear short sentences from their children as easily as long ones. Notice, too, that Nehemiah’s quick prayer rested on months of longer ones. The two feed each other. But when all you have is a breath, a breath is enough. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> God of heaven, thank you that you hear the prayers I manage between meetings — the stairwell sentences, the one-word pleas. Teach me to aim those breaths at you all day long. Let the short prayers keep me honest and the long ones keep me rooted. And when the stakes are highest and the time is shortest, pray in me what I cannot compose. <break time="1.1s" /> I will send up short prayers between meetings today and trust that they count. <break time="1.1s" /> Move through your crowded day breathing prayers upward, for the God of heaven hears every one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-sc-feed: On the Word Before the Feed. <break time="1.8s" /> The phone is within reach, and the day is already asking for you. Before you pick it up, let another voice speak first. <break time="1.1s" /> “I rise before dawn and cry for help; I have put my hope in your word.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 119, verse 147. <break time="1.1s" /> Whatever you read first in the morning tells you what the day is about. The feed has a story ready before your feet hit the floor: someone else’s launch, someone else’s round, three fires in your inbox, and the quiet suggestion that you are already behind. It is not that the phone is evil. It is that it always speaks first, and whoever speaks first sets the terms. The psalmist rose before dawn not to be impressive but because he had decided where his hope lived — “I have put my hope in your word.” Notice what he reached for. Not a strategy, not a report on his standing, but a word from the God who loved him. That is the difference the first few minutes make. The feed tells you what you must do to matter today. The Word tells you that you already matter, before you have produced anything, because you are Christ’s. Founders especially need to hear that before they hear anything else. Let the news of grace be older than the news of the day. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you know how fast my hand goes to the phone and how slowly it goes to your Word. Speak first tomorrow morning; let your voice set the terms of my day. Teach me to put my hope where the psalmist put his. Meet me before the noise does. <break time="1.1s" /> I will open the Word before I open the feed tomorrow morning, even if only for a few minutes. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into this day with God’s word as the first word, and let every other voice come second. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-sc-slow: On Reading Slowly. <break time="1.8s" /> You skim for a living — decks, threads, dashboards. For these few minutes, put the skimming down and read at the speed of a person listening. <break time="1.1s" /> “…whose delight is in the law of the Lord, and who meditates on his law day and night. That person is like a tree planted by streams of water, which yields its fruit in season and whose leaf does not wither.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 1, verses 2 to 3. <break time="1.1s" /> Skimming is a founder’s survival skill. You learn to extract the point in seconds and move on, because there is always more to get through. But Scripture does not yield to extraction, and the psalm quietly explains why. The blessed life is not pictured as a processor of information but as a tree planted by streams — and trees do not gulp. They stay put and draw water slowly, through roots, over seasons. Meditation is the reading that matches that picture: the same few verses turned over, reread, murmured, questioned, until they stop being content and start being water. Notice too the word delight. This is not homework assigned by a distant God; it is a table set by a Father who wants to be known. You can skim a memo from a stranger, but you linger over a letter from someone who loves you. So take less and read it more. One psalm, slowly, will feed you longer than three chapters at scroll speed — and in season, without your forcing it, there will be fruit. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I confess I read your Word the way I read everything else — fast, and looking for the takeaway. Slow me down. Give me delight where I have only had discipline, and roots where I have only had speed. Plant me by the stream and keep me there. <break time="1.1s" /> I will read tomorrow’s passage twice, slowly, and sit with one line instead of rushing to finish. <break time="1.1s" /> Go slowly into a fast day, rooted like a tree by water that does not run dry. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-sc-carry: On Carrying One Verse. <break time="1.8s" /> Be honest: can you remember what you read yesterday morning? Come quietly, and consider how a verse might walk with you instead of waving goodbye at the door. <break time="1.1s" /> “Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. Then you will be prosperous and successful.” <break time="1.1s" />Joshua 1, verse 8. <break time="1.1s" /> God did not tell Joshua to have a quiet time. He told him to keep the Word on his lips — day and night, in the camp and on the march, while the actual work of leading actual people went on. The reading was never meant to stay in the morning. It was meant to travel. For you, that might be as simple as this: before you close the Bible, take one verse with you. Write it on a sticky note, put it at the top of today’s to-do list, let it interrupt you between meetings the way notifications already do. A verse carried into a hard negotiation or a tense one-on-one does more than a chapter left at the kitchen table. And do not misread the promise at the end. The prosperity held out to Joshua was not a growth metric; it was God’s own presence going with him into the land. That is still the offer. The Word you carry is how the God who speaks it stays near — through the standup, the pitch, and the long afternoon. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I keep leaving your Word behind with the breakfast dishes. Give me one verse today and keep it on my lips. Bring it back to me in the moments when I most need to remember who you are. Walk with me through the workday, not just the quiet one. <break time="1.1s" /> I will choose one verse from my reading each morning and carry it visibly into the workday. <break time="1.1s" /> Go with the Word on your lips, and let it speak in the rooms where your day is decided. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-sc-dry: On Dry Seasons in the Word. <break time="1.8s" /> You opened the Book again and felt nothing again. Stay anyway, for a few minutes, and hear what God says his word is doing while you feel dry. <break time="1.1s" /> “As the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and do not return to it without watering the earth and making it bud and flourish … so is my word that goes out from my mouth: It will not return to me empty, but will accomplish what I desire and achieve the purpose for which I sent it.” <break time="1.1s" />Isaiah 55, verses 10 to 11. <break time="1.1s" /> Founders live by dashboards, so when Scripture stops producing a feeling, it is natural to conclude the channel is dead and quietly stop. But notice the picture God chooses for his word: not lightning, rain. Rain is unglamorous. It falls on soil that looks exactly the same afterward, and the watering happens out of sight, in the dark, where roots are. No farmer stands in a drizzle demanding to feel the harvest. God stakes his own name on the outcome — my word will not return to me empty — and he does not add “provided the reader feels something.” The work is his, not yours; that is the shape of grace, in reading as in everything else. Dryness is not evidence of failure. Often it is simply a season, and seasons are where fruit comes from. So keep showing up with your unspectacular ten minutes. You are not performing devotion for an unimpressed audience; you are soil under faithful rain. One morning, further on than you expected, something green will surprise you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, your Word feels dry to me right now, and I confess I am tempted to quit. Thank you that your rain does its work whether or not I feel it fall. Keep me in the field; keep the Book open in front of me. Bring the green shoots in your own time. <break time="1.1s" /> I will keep my reading time this week even when I feel nothing, trusting the Word to do its quiet work. <break time="1.1s" /> Go on through the dry season, and trust the rain that never returns empty. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-sc-small: On Starting Small and Staying. <break time="1.8s" /> You have started ambitious plans before, and busy weeks have buried them. Set the ambition down for a moment and consider something smaller — and more like bread. <break time="1.1s" /> “Jesus answered, ‘It is written: “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.”’” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 4, verse 4. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus compares the Word to bread, and the comparison is instruction. Nobody eats heroically. You do not consume a week of food on Sunday and coast; you eat something small, most days, for your whole life. Yet founders approach Scripture the way they approach everything — with a bold plan, front-loaded intensity, and a quiet collapse by week three, followed by enough guilt to delay the next attempt. Bread suggests another way. Shrink the habit until it is almost embarrassing: five verses with your coffee, one psalm before you open the laptop. A portion so small that a brutal day cannot dislodge it. This is not settling for less; it is how sustenance actually works, and it is also how grace works. Your Father is not grading the size of your servings. He is feeding you, and he is glad you came to the table at all. Miss a day? Eat the next one — no penance, no starting the plan over from zero. Small and kept will outfeed grand and abandoned, every time. Ten years of crumbs is a feast. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, forgive my heroic plans and my quiet quitting, and teach me the humility of bread. Give me a portion of your Word small enough to keep and rich enough to live on. When I miss a day, bring me back without shame. Feed me daily, as you promised. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pick a portion of Scripture small enough to survive my worst day, and read it tomorrow. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and eat your daily bread — small, steady, and enough for today. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-gv-model:
On Building Giving In. <break time="1.8s" /> Come and consider how your business is built, not just what it earns. God has a word for founders who design the harvest. <break time="1.1s" /> “When you reap the harvest of your land, do not reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest. Do not go over your vineyard a second time or pick up the grapes that have fallen. Leave them for the poor and the foreigner. I am the Lord your God.” <break time="1.1s" />Leviticus 19, verses 9 to 10. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice when this command arrives: before the harvest, not after it. Israel’s farmers were told to design generosity into the field itself — unreaped edges, ungathered gleanings — so that giving was never a question of leftover mood or leftover margin. It was architecture. The poor were fed not by a farmer’s occasional surge of feeling but by the shape of his rows.

Most founders intend to be generous someday, once the numbers settle. But “someday” is where good intentions go to retire. If giving lives only in your leftovers, it will always be negotiable, and negotiable things lose to payroll every time. The invitation here is quieter and sturdier: build the edge into the field. A percentage in the operating plan. A line item that exists before the forecast does. Pro bono hours on the actual calendar.

And underneath the practice is a gospel logic — the whole field was God’s gift before you reaped a single row. You are not carving generosity out of what is yours; you are leaving room in what was always his. Grace came to you built-in, not as an afterthought. Build your field the same way. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, every field I work was yours before I ever touched it. Forgive me for treating generosity as a bonus feature instead of a load-bearing wall. Help me design giving into the structure of this business, where no bad quarter can quietly delete it. Make my company a field with edges left unreaped. <break time="1.1s" /> I will write one concrete act of giving into my operating plan this week — a percentage, a line item, or scheduled hours — so it exists before the leftovers do. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and build the edges of your field for someone who will never see your spreadsheet. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-gv-credit:
On Giving Away the Credit. <break time="1.8s" /> Come, you who hunger to be recognized. There is a generosity that costs nothing from your bank account and everything from your ego. <break time="1.1s" /> “He must become greater; I must become less.” <break time="1.1s" />John 3, verse 30. <break time="1.1s" /> John the Baptist had every claim to the credit. He drew the crowds first — the voice in the wilderness, the baptizer of thousands, the one with the following. Yet when his own disciples came to him anxious that everyone was now leaving for Jesus, he answered with one of the freest sentences in Scripture: he must become greater; I must become less. He hands over the spotlight in a single breath, and calls the handover joy.

Money is not the only currency a founder controls. You also hold credit and opportunity — whose name goes on the win, who presents to the board, who gets the stretch project that could make a career. These can be hoarded as easily as cash, and hoarded more invisibly. Nobody audits who absorbed the spotlight.

But generosity with credit is generosity all the same, and it may be the kind that costs you most. Praise feels like oxygen when you are building something fragile. The gospel loosens that grip: your significance was settled at the cross, not at the all-hands. You do not need the applause, because you already have the verdict — beloved, before you shipped anything. From that security, credit becomes something you can hand away gladly, as John did. Shine it on someone junior and watch what God makes of them. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you know how tightly I hold recognition, and how much of my hunger for credit is really hunger for assurance. Settle me in your verdict over my life, so applause becomes something I can pass along instead of collect. Show me one person this week whose work deserves the light I have been standing in. Make me glad, not grudging, when their name is spoken instead of mine. <break time="1.1s" /> I will publicly credit a specific person for a specific win this week, and hand someone junior an opportunity I could have kept for myself. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and spend your spotlight on someone who has never stood in one. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-gv-thin:
On Giving from Thin Margins. <break time="1.8s" /> Come, you who are watching runway shrink and wondering if generosity is a luxury for later. Scripture has seen thinner margins than yours. <break time="1.1s" /> “In the midst of a very severe trial, their overflowing joy and their extreme poverty welled up in rich generosity. For I testify that they gave as much as they were able, and even beyond their ability.” <break time="1.1s" />2 Corinthians 8, verses 2 to 3. <break time="1.1s" /> The Macedonian churches had none of the preconditions we assume generosity requires. Severe trial. Extreme poverty. And yet Paul describes their giving with a word we reserve for flooded rivers: it welled up. Their generosity was not the overflow of surplus; it was the overflow of joy, and joy does not check the balance first.

This is not a demand that you give recklessly while your team’s paychecks hang in the balance — Scripture also honors the founder who counts the cost. It is something gentler and more unsettling: proof that thin margins do not disqualify you. If generosity only counts when it is easy, the Macedonians would have been excused. Instead they became the example.

When money is tight, giving becomes a confession — a way of saying, out loud and on the ledger, that God is my provider and not my pipeline. Even a small gift in a hard season does something a large gift in a fat season cannot: it breaks fear’s grip on your hands. Paul roots it all in Christ, who though he was rich, for your sake became poor. Your thinnest margin sits inside that wealth. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you see the numbers that keep me up at night, and you see how scarcity is teaching my hands to close. I confess I have made giving conditional on comfort. Loosen my grip, even a little, in this lean season. Let one small act of generosity declare that you, not my revenue, are holding me up. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give one specific gift this month — sized honestly to this season, but real — before the numbers tell me I am allowed to. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and let a small gift in a lean season say what a large one never could. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-gv-knowledge:
On Open-Handed Knowledge. <break time="1.8s" /> Come and take inventory of everything you know that someone once taught you for free. Then ask why your own hands have closed. <break time="1.1s" /> “…Freely you have received; freely give.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 10, verse 8. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus sends out the Twelve with power they did not earn, and gives them one rule for its use: freely you have received; freely give. What came to you as gift may not leave you as merchandise.

Think honestly about how you learned this trade. The engineer who let you shadow her. The founder two years ahead who took your panicked call at 10 p.m. The blog post that saved you a ruinous mistake, written by someone who gained nothing from your rescue. Almost nothing you know arrived full price. Yet somewhere along the way, knowledge started to feel like the moat — the one asset that must be guarded, especially from competitors and their people.

So here is a strange discipline: mentor a junior from a rival firm. Write down the lesson that cost you a year and publish it. Answer the cold email from the kid building something suspiciously like your product. This is not naivety about competition; it is defiance of the scarcity story. The economy of God runs on seed, not silos — what is sown multiplies, what is hoarded molds. You received freely. Keep the current moving. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, thank you for every person who taught me for nothing, and forgive me for pricing what I was handed as a gift. Free me from the fear that sharing what I know will shrink what I have. Give me eyes for one hungry learner — even a competitor’s — whom I can help this month. Make my knowledge a river, not a reservoir. <break time="1.1s" /> I will share one hard-won lesson openly this month — a mentoring hour, a written post, or a returned cold email — with someone who can do nothing for me in return. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and teach someone the thing that cost you the most to learn. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-gv-quiet:
On the Quiet Gift. <break time="1.8s" /> Come away from the metrics for a moment, you who measure everything. Some of the truest work of your life will never appear on a dashboard. <break time="1.1s" /> “But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.” <break time="1.1s" />Matthew 6, verses 3 to 4. <break time="1.1s" /> Founders live in public. Your wins are announced, your funding is covered, even your giving can become content — the check enlarged for the camera, the partnership wrapped in a press release. Jesus does not condemn giving that happens to be seen. He warns against giving engineered to be seen, because an audience quietly changes what a gift is. Performed generosity is a transaction; you gave, and applause paid you back in full.

The secret gift is different in kind, not just in volume. When you cover a struggling vendor’s invoice and tell no one, forgive a debt without a LinkedIn post, slip severance beyond obligation to someone who will never trace it — you discover what your generosity is actually made of. Secrecy is the assay that separates love from marketing.

And you are not unseen. Your Father, who sees what is done in secret — that is the astonishing center of the verse. The God of the universe watches the gift nobody claps for, and calls it treasure. Build one hidden channel of giving into your life as a founder. Let it stay hidden. It may become the freest thing you own. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, so much of my life is performed that I hardly know how to do a thing quietly anymore. Teach me the freedom of the gift that earns no post, no thanks, no strategic goodwill. Give me one secret generosity to carry, and the strength to keep it secret. It is enough that you see. <break time="1.1s" /> I will give one gift this week that no one but God will ever know about, and I will tell no one. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and hide one act of generosity where only your Father will find it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-in-fudge: On the Numbers That Round Up. <break time="1.8s" /> Before you send the update or share the dashboard, pause over the numbers. Ask whether each one is true, or merely useful. <break time="1.1s" /> “Honest scales and balances belong to the Lord; all the weights in the bag are of his making.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 16, verse 11. <break time="1.1s" /> In the ancient market, a merchant carried his weights in a bag, and a dishonest one carried two sets — one for buying, one for selling. No customer could see inside the bag. That is exactly where this proverb locates God: among the weights. The scales themselves belong to him. Founders carry their weights in dashboards and investor updates. ‘Almost ten thousand users’ when it is eight-something. A conversion rate quoted from the best week. Churn measured the flattering way. Each rounding feels like presentation, not deception — but a shaved weight is a shaved weight, and the person reading your deck is buying with it. Here is the deeper mercy: you fudge numbers when you believe the numbers are what will save you — that funding, credibility, survival all hang on the slope of a chart. They don’t. Your future is held by the God who owns the scales, which means you can afford accuracy. The real number, honestly told, may be smaller than you wish. It is also solid ground, and you can build on it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you own the scales I weigh my company on. Forgive me for the roundings that flatter me and mislead others. Give me the courage to report what is, not what I wish were true. Teach me to trust you with the smaller, truer number. <break time="1.1s" /> I will report my numbers exactly as they are, even when the true figure is less impressive. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and weigh honestly — the God who owns the scales can be trusted with the total. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-in-costly: On Truth That Costs the Deal. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere today a question may come whose honest answer could cost you money. Settle now which answer you will give. <break time="1.1s" /> “Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 12, verse 19. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a moment in almost every deal when the honest sentence and the winning sentence part ways. The feature is not built yet. The timeline is optimistic. The integration they are counting on is fragile. You can feel the deal lean on your answer, and the tempting words are technically defensible. Notice that the proverb does not pretend lies never work — it says they last only a moment. The dishonest close works right up until onboarding, and then it becomes a churned customer, a burned reference, a support fire, and a story told about you in rooms you will never enter. Truthful lips endure; so does a company built by them. And see what telling the costly truth actually is: a small act of faith. It says out loud that you believe God can grow this business without your embellishment — that you would rather lose the deal than lose yourself. Some prospects will walk. The ones who stay will trust you in a way no pitch could manufacture, because they watched you choose them over the close. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I confess how much I want the deal, and how flexible the truth becomes when I want something. Steady me before the moment comes. Let me answer honestly even while I watch the revenue walk out the door. I trust you to build this company without my embellishment. <break time="1.1s" /> I will tell the whole truth in today’s conversations, even if it costs me the deal. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and speak plainly — what is built on truthful lips endures. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-in-gray: On What Everyone Else Does. <break time="1.8s" /> Name, just to yourself, one practice in your industry that everyone accepts and no one examines. Hold it up to the light for these few minutes. <break time="1.1s" /> “Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is — his good, pleasing and perfect will.” <break time="1.1s" />Romans 12, verse 2. <break time="1.1s" /> Every industry has its patterns — the inflated ‘active user’ definition, the auto-renewal buried at checkout, the reference customer who was quietly comped, the standard practice everyone shrugs about. Nobody calls it lying. It is just the water. That is precisely what Paul means by the pattern of this world: not cartoonish evil, but the ordinary shape everyone’s conduct settles into until it seems like physics. Conforming never feels like a decision — that is what makes it a pattern. Transformation, by contrast, begins in the mind: a renewed ability to look at what everyone does and actually test it, rather than inherit it. Notice the promise attached to the command — then you will be able to discern what is good. The gray resolves as the mind is renewed. You do not have to become the industry’s scold, auditing everyone else’s ethics. You only have to be quietly unconformed, running your own shop by what survives testing. The gospel makes that possible, because your belonging is already settled in Christ. You do not need the industry’s pattern to hold you; you were bought out of it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I have inherited habits from my industry without ever testing them. Renew my mind until I can see the water I swim in. Show me the accepted practice you are asking me to leave behind. Give me the quiet nerve to be different without being self-righteous. <break time="1.1s" /> I will test one accepted industry practice against what is actually true and fair, instead of inheriting it. <break time="1.1s" /> Go unconformed — let the renewed mind, not the industry, set the pattern. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-in-word: On Keeping Your Word. <break time="1.8s" /> Bring to mind a promise you made when it was cheap that has since grown expensive. Sit with it honestly before God. <break time="1.1s" /> “When you make a vow to God, do not delay to fulfill it. He has no pleasure in fools; fulfill your vow. It is better not to make a vow than to make one and not fulfill it.” <break time="1.1s" />Ecclesiastes 5, verses 4 to 5. <break time="1.1s" /> The Teacher’s counsel is blunt: better never to promise than to promise and not deliver. He speaks of vows made to God, but every promise a founder makes is made in God’s hearing — and notice what the verse assumes: that between the making of a vow and the keeping of it, something will tempt you to delay, to let it quietly lapse. You quoted a price before your costs rose. You promised a hire equity before the plan changed. You made a customer a commitment the new strategy finds inconvenient. The circumstances genuinely changed; that part is true. But your word was given precisely so that people would not have to keep watching the circumstances. That is what a promise is for. When keeping it costs you, you are not simply losing money — you are buying something: the kind of name that lets people rest when you speak. And you are echoing the God you serve, who made covenant knowing exactly what it would cost him, and kept it at a cross. Where a promise truly cannot be kept, honor it in the open: go to the person, own it, and make it right — never quietly redefine it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you are the God who keeps covenant at your own expense. I want to be like you in my small dealings. Strengthen me to keep the promise that has grown expensive, and humble me to go openly to anyone whose promise I cannot keep. Make my word a place where people can rest. <break time="1.1s" /> I will keep the commitment I made even though circumstances have changed, or go honestly to the person it affects. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and fulfill what your lips have promised — you serve a God who kept his word at a cross. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-in-unseen: On the Unwatched Hours. <break time="1.8s" /> Think of the parts of your work no employee ever sees — the inbox, the expenses, the late-night decisions. Invite God into that room first. <break time="1.1s" /> “Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” <break time="1.1s" />Psalm 139, verses 23 to 24. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a version of you that shows up when the team is watching — patient in the all-hands, principled in the interview, generous in the retro. And there is the founder alone with the admin dashboard, the expense report, the private message thread, the vendor who will never talk to your staff. Culture is not what you announce; it is what you are in that second room, because a company eventually becomes its founder’s private habits made public. David’s prayer is striking because it runs in the opposite direction from hiding: search me. Know my heart. He invites the audit. And he can do it only because the Searcher is not a hostile inspector but the God who, a few verses earlier, knit him together and hems him in with love. That is the gospel’s strange comfort — you are already fully seen and still fully loved, so there is nothing left to protect by pretending. The unwatched hours stop being a place to get away with things and become a place to be formed. What God finds in the second room, he does not expose; he heals. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> God, you already see the rooms no one on my team enters. Search me there — I open the door instead of guarding it. Show me the private habit that does not match my public self. Form me in the unwatched hours until I am one person everywhere. <break time="1.1s" /> I will act in today’s unseen moments exactly as I would if the whole team were in the room. <break time="1.1s" /> Go fully seen and fully loved — and let the unwatched hours make you whole. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-wt-hidden: On the Hidden Season. <break time="1.8s" /> Come away from the dashboard for a moment. The God who grows seed in the dark is at work in your quiet season. <break time="1.1s" /> “This is what the kingdom of God is like. A man scatters seed on the ground. Night and day, whether he sleeps or gets up, the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how.” <break time="1.1s" />Mark 4, verses 26 to 27. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus told of a farmer who scatters seed and then, remarkably, goes to bed. Night and day the man sleeps and rises, and the seed grows — he doesn’t know how, and he doesn’t need to. You know the season this parable describes: the outreach is sent, the product is shipped, the pipeline is built, and the dashboard sits stubbornly flat. Nothing visible is happening. But farming, Jesus insists, is the shape of the kingdom, and in farming the most important work is invisible. Underground, in the dark, out of sight of every metric, the seed is doing exactly what seeds do. It is worth remembering that God himself worked this way: thirty hidden years in Nazareth before a single public miracle, a salvation accomplished in a sealed tomb while the world saw nothing. God is not idle when he is invisible. The quiet weeks are not the absence of the story. They are the chapter where the roots go down — the one no one reads but everything depends on. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I confess I equate your activity with visible progress. Teach me the patience of the farmer who sleeps because he trusts the seed. Work in the hidden places of this company, and in the hidden places of me. Help me believe you are moving when I can see nothing. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name one hidden thing God may be growing right now and thank him for it before I check my metrics today. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and rest tonight like the farmer, trusting the God who grows seed in the dark. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-wt-outofhands: On What Is Out of Your Hands. <break time="1.8s" /> Set down the phone you keep checking. The decision you’re waiting on rests in hands steadier than the ones that will sign it. <break time="1.1s" /> “In the Lord’s hand the king’s heart is a stream of water that he channels toward all who please him.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 21, verse 1. <break time="1.1s" /> Proverbs reaches for the most immovable decision-maker its world knew — the king, answerable to no one — and says his heart is a stream of water in the Lord’s hand. Not a boulder to be shoved; a stream to be channeled. You are waiting on someone like that. An investor who has gone quiet, a counterparty sitting on a signature, a regulator whose timeline answers to nobody. You have sent the follow-up. There is nothing left to do, and that is precisely the ache. This verse doesn’t promise the yes. It promises something sturdier: that no decision on earth is made outside the reach of God’s hand. Even the most crooked verdict in history — a Roman governor signing off on the death of an innocent man — was channeled into the salvation of the world. If God can work through that signature, he can be trusted with the one you’re waiting on. Your task now is not to grip harder but to release: the outcome was never in your hands, and it was always in better ones. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, this decision is out of my hands, and I keep pretending otherwise. I place the investor, the signature, the answer into your hands, where they already were. Give me peace while I wait, and grace to trust you with either answer. Keep my heart soft toward the people I’m waiting on. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pray for the person whose decision I’m waiting on, by name, before I follow up again. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into this day with open hands, trusting the One who channels rivers and hearts. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-wt-planting: On Planting for Distant Harvests. <break time="1.8s" /> Lift your eyes past this quarter. Some of what you plant today is meant for a harvest you may never see. <break time="1.1s" /> “Thus the saying ‘One sows and another reaps’ is true. I sent you to reap what you have not worked for. Others have done the hard work, and you have reaped the benefits of their labor.” <break time="1.1s" />John 4, verses 37 to 38. <break time="1.1s" /> Jesus, watching a Samaritan village stream toward him, told his disciples they were harvesting a field they had never worked: one sows and another reaps, and others have done the hard work before you. It is a humbling arithmetic, and a freeing one. Some of the best work you will ever do won’t show up in this year’s numbers, or next year’s. The culture you set, the trust you build with customers, the junior you patiently mentor, the corners you refuse to cut — these are seeds with long germination. Some will bear fruit after you’ve moved on, in a harvest carried in by someone else’s hands. Founders are trained to want the sowing and the reaping in the same quarter. Jesus tells a longer story, in which one sows and another reaps and both rejoice together at the same harvest. Your part is faithful planting. So plant generously, tend honestly, and let go of the timeline — the reaping was never promised to your quarter, and the harvest was never only for you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> God of the harvest, forgive my hurry to reap everything I sow. Give me the faith to plant what I may never see mature. Make me generous with work whose reward belongs to someone else. I trust you with the reaping. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do one piece of long-horizon work today that no metric will reward this quarter. <break time="1.1s" /> Plant today what another generation may harvest, and be glad. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-wt-forcing: On Forcing Doors. <break time="1.8s" /> Step back from the door you’ve been pushing. Come and learn the strength that waits. <break time="1.1s" /> “In repentance and rest is your salvation, in quietness and trust is your strength, but you would have none of it.” <break time="1.1s" />Isaiah 30, verse 15. <break time="1.1s" /> Israel, under threat, wanted to gallop down to Egypt and buy horses — a fast, forceful, sensible-looking plan. God’s counter-offer sounded almost insulting by comparison: in repentance and rest is your salvation, in quietness and trust is your strength. But you would have none of it, the verse adds, and the words sting because we know the feeling. There is a version of this for every founder staring at a closed door: pressure the investor, massage the metric, take the money you know is misaligned, ship what you know isn’t ready. Forced doors do open sometimes — and they have a way of closing on your fingers later. Quietness is not passivity. It is the strenuous discipline of not reaching for the crowbar, because you believe God doesn’t need your shortcut to keep his promises. Jesus faced this exact temptation in the wilderness: all the kingdoms of the world, without the cross, right now. He waited instead. Every door the Father opened for him stayed open — and his patience is both the pattern and the power for yours. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you know which door I’ve been trying to force. I am tired of pushing, and afraid of what waiting might cost me. Give me the quietness and trust you promise are my strength. Keep me from any yes I would have to manufacture myself. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name the door I’ve been forcing and lay down one tactic I know is a crowbar. <break time="1.1s" /> Wait at the door in quietness and trust, and let God be the one to open it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-wt-formed: On What Waiting Makes of You. <break time="1.8s" /> The waiting is not wasted on you. Come and see what God is making of it. <break time="1.1s" /> “Let perseverance finish its work so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.” <break time="1.1s" />James 1, verse 4. <break time="1.1s" /> James asks something strange of people in hard seasons: let perseverance finish its work. Finish — as if the waiting itself were a craftsman partway through a project, and the project is you. Here is the truth that arriving can never teach: if the term sheet had come the day you asked, you would have the money but not the muscle. Delay is where founders learn to pray honestly, to lead without applause, to separate their worth from their metrics, to trust God in the dark. None of that is available on the far side of the yes; it is forged only in the middle. Mature and complete, not lacking anything — it is a startling promise to make to people who feel they lack everything: funding, traction, certainty. Yet James means it. God is doing his deepest work in you precisely where nothing seems to be happening, and he is more committed to who you are becoming than to your timeline. The wait is not the obstacle to the work. Often, it is the work. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I have treated this waiting season as an enemy. Thank you that you are forming something in me that arriving never could. Let perseverance finish its work, even when I want to rush it. Make me the kind of person who can carry what I’m asking for. <break time="1.1s" /> I will write down one way this waiting season has already changed me for the better. <break time="1.1s" /> Stay in the waiting with hope, and let perseverance finish its good work in you. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-cr-ask: On the Ask You Keep Postponing. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere on your list is an ask you keep moving to tomorrow. Bring it into the light before God, and let him ask you why. <break time="1.1s" /> “For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place … And who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?” <break time="1.1s" />Esther 4, verse 14. <break time="1.1s" /> Mordecai does not flatter Esther into courage. He tells her the truth: silence is also a choice, and deliverance does not depend on her — relief will arise from another place. That is strangely freeing. The ask you keep postponing — the investor call, the price increase, the customer you need to phone — has come to feel enormous, as though everything hangs on it. It doesn’t. God’s purposes will not collapse if you fumble the words. But Mordecai adds a second truth: perhaps you were placed here, in this seat, with this access, for exactly this moment. Postponement usually isn’t about the calendar; it is about protecting ourselves from a no. The gospel loosens that grip. In Christ you already have the yes that matters most, secured before you ever pitched anything, so a rejection can bruise you but it cannot define you. Esther fasted, then walked toward the throne room. Notice the order: she brought her fear to God first, then made the ask anyway. Whatever you have been circling for weeks — today is a fine day to stop circling. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you know the ask I keep postponing, and you know the fear underneath it. Thank you that your purposes do not hang on my performance, and that in Christ I already have the yes that matters most. Give me the courage to stop circling and to say the words plainly. Whatever the answer, keep my heart quiet in you. <break time="1.1s" /> I will make the ask I have been postponing this week — and I will pray before I pick up the phone. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and ask plainly, for the answer that defines you has already been given in Christ. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-cr-obedience: On Courage as Obedience. <break time="1.8s" /> You may be waiting for a feeling of bravery that is not coming. Be still for a moment, and listen instead for an instruction. <break time="1.1s" /> “‘Be strong, all you people of the land,’ declares the Lord, ‘and work. For I am with you,’ declares the Lord Almighty.” <break time="1.1s" />Haggai 2, verse 4. <break time="1.1s" /> Haggai speaks to people rebuilding a temple that looks embarrassing next to the one they remember. They are not charging a hill; they are hauling stones, discouraged, midway through a project that has lost its shine. And God’s word to them is not a pep talk but a command with a promise inside it: be strong — and work. For I am with you. Notice what courage is here. Not a surge of feeling. Not the founder’s adrenaline of launch day, which burns off by the following Tuesday. Courage in Scripture is almost always this: doing the assigned thing, again, because God is present in it. That reframes your week. You do not need to feel brave to send the difficult email, hold the standard, or keep building through the unglamorous middle. You need to obey the next clear instruction, and the feeling can catch up whenever it likes — or not. The presence of God, not the presence of confidence, is the ground under a courageous life. Adrenaline asks, “How do I feel?” Obedience asks, “What has he said?” — and then it picks the tools back up. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, I confess I have been waiting to feel brave, and the feeling has not come. Teach me that your presence, not my confidence, is the ground I stand on. Show me the next act of plain obedience in front of me today. Make me strong enough to simply do it, whether or not my heart races. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do the next thing God has put in front of me today without waiting to feel brave first. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and do the assigned work, for the Lord Almighty is with you in it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-cr-reputation: On Risking Your Name. <break time="1.8s" /> There may be a room this week where the honest thing will cost you something. Sit before God now, before you walk into it. <break time="1.1s" /> “If we are thrown into the blazing furnace, the God we serve is able to deliver us from it … But even if he does not, we want you to know, Your Majesty, that we will not serve your gods or worship the image of gold you have set up.” <break time="1.1s" />Daniel 3, verses 17 to 18. <break time="1.1s" /> What steadies Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego is not certainty that they will be spared. It is the settled decision that God’s verdict outweighs the king’s — but even if he does not. They risk their positions, their reputations at court, their very lives, without any guarantee of rescue, because some things are not for sale. Founders rarely face furnaces, but we face rooms: the board meeting where the honest number will disappoint, the customer who deserves the refund, the deal we should decline though everyone says take it. In those rooms your reputation feels like the whole asset — hard-won, fragile, compounding. And the quiet lie is that God needs your polished name to accomplish his purposes, so a little compromise is really stewardship. It isn’t. The gospel says your truest name is already secure — hidden with Christ, not held by the market — so you can spend your reputation on the truth without going bankrupt. Perhaps God will vindicate you quickly; he often does. But even if he does not, you will walk out of that room with the one thing a furnace cannot take. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, you know how carefully I have built my name, and how afraid I am to spend it. Settle in me the conviction that your verdict outweighs every room I will ever stand in. Give me the courage to tell the truth and do what is right, even without a guarantee of rescue. Hide my reputation with Christ, where no loss can reach it. <break time="1.1s" /> I will do the right thing in the room I have been dreading, and leave my reputation in God’s keeping. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and tell the truth, even if he does not deliver you the way you hoped, for your name is safe with him. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-cr-reckless: On Faith and Recklessness. <break time="1.8s" /> Not every leap is holy, and not every hesitation is fear. Ask God to help you tell the difference before you jump. <break time="1.1s" /> “But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to meet this threat.” <break time="1.1s" />Nehemiah 4, verse 9. <break time="1.1s" /> Nehemiah’s wall-builders were under threat, and his response is a single sentence that holds the whole tension: we prayed to our God and posted a guard. Not prayer instead of a guard. Not a guard instead of prayer. Faith and diligence in the same breath. This is the line between holy risk and recklessness, and it is worth learning, because from the outside the two can look identical — bold, fast, exposed. Recklessness skips the guard: it ignores the runway math, avoids counsel, bets the company to feel alive or to escape a slow problem. Faith-risk prays and then does the sober work: it counts the cost, tells the truth about the odds, and still moves when obedience requires it. Here is a test: can you name the obedience in the risk you are weighing — or only the upside? Recklessness borrows the vocabulary of faith to dodge diligence; faith wears work gloves. God is not honored when we call our impatience trust. But neither is he honored by a caution that is really unbelief with a spreadsheet. So pray. Post the guard. Then build the wall in the open. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, help me tell the difference between the risk you are asking of me and the gamble my restlessness wants. Keep me from calling impatience faith, and from calling unbelief prudence. Give me the humility to count the cost and seek counsel, and the courage to move when you say move. Let both my praying and my planning honor you. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name the obedience in the risk I am weighing before I take it — and pray and plan in the same breath. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and take the risks obedience requires — praying like Nehemiah, and posting the guard. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-cr-first: On Going First. <break time="1.8s" /> Your team’s courage is largely borrowed from yours. Sit with the step you have been asking others to take without taking it yourself. <break time="1.1s" /> “Jonathan said to his young armor-bearer, ‘Come, let’s go over to the outpost … Perhaps the Lord will act in our behalf. Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few.’” <break time="1.1s" />1 Samuel 14, verse 6. <break time="1.1s" /> Jonathan does not send scouts. He climbs the rocks toward the Philistine outpost on his own hands and feet, first, with one companion behind him. And notice his theology: “Perhaps the Lord will act in our behalf.” Perhaps. Not presumption — he claims no guarantee — but a confidence that nothing can hinder the Lord from saving, by many or by few. His armor-bearer’s answer is the fruit of that kind of leading: “Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul.” Nobody says that to a leader who only points. Your team’s courage is largely borrowed, and they can only borrow what you have actually spent. If you want them to make bold asks, they need to hear you make one and survive the no. If you want honesty in the retrospective, yours goes first. Going first is a small crucifixion — you absorb the risk so that others can move. Which is to say, it is the shape of Christ, who did not manage our redemption from a distance but went ahead of us, through death itself, so that following could feel like walking a cleared path. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, forgive me for the times I have pointed at risks instead of taking them. Thank you that Jesus went first through the hardest ground, so that I follow a cleared path. Give me Jonathan’s humble confidence — no guarantees, but full trust that nothing can hinder you. Make my courage something my team can borrow. <break time="1.1s" /> I will take the first visible step on the thing I have been asking my team to be brave about. <break time="1.1s" /> Go first up the rocks, and let those who follow find the path already walked. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-hu-junior: On Listening Down. <break time="1.8s" /> Come, you who sit at the top of the org chart. Wisdom is speaking today, and it has not checked anyone’s title. <break time="1.1s" /> “Listen to advice and accept discipline, and at the end you will be counted among the wise.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 19, verse 20. <break time="1.1s" /> Wisdom, in Proverbs, never checks credentials. “Listen to advice and accept discipline” — the verse does not say whose advice, because it does not matter. What matters is the listening. Yet something in a founder resists counsel that travels upward: the engineer two years out of school, the intern who noticed what you missed. Taking their advice can feel like admitting the org chart is a fiction — and in the kingdom of God, it mostly is. God has a long habit of speaking through the unlikely: a shepherd boy, a servant girl, a carpenter’s son from Nazareth whom the credentialed experts dismissed. If your identity rests on being the source of every good idea, junior wisdom will feel like a threat. But if your identity rests in Christ — loved before you shipped anything — then a better idea from the newest hire is not a demotion; it is a gift. Proverbs says the listener is counted wise “at the end.” Humility is a long game. The founders still standing in ten years are usually the ones who learned, early, to hear truth from anyone. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I confess that I weigh advice by the rank of the person giving it. Forgive my deafness to the voices you have placed below me on a chart you never drew. Settle my identity so deeply in Christ that a better idea feels like a gift and not a threat. Give me ears today for wisdom, wherever you send it from. <break time="1.1s" /> I will ask the most junior person on my team what they would change, and listen without defending. <break time="1.1s" /> Go into your day with open ears, and let wisdom find you through whomever God chooses. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-hu-wrong: On Saying It Out Loud. <break time="1.8s" /> Come with the mistake you are still holding behind your back. Mercy is waiting on the other side of plain words. <break time="1.1s" /> “Whoever conceals their sins does not prosper, but the one who confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 28, verse 13. <break time="1.1s" /> There is a moment after you realize you were wrong — before anyone else names it — when two roads open. One is management: reframe, redirect, let the mistake blur into “learnings.” The other is confession: plain words, in front of the people who watched you insist. Proverbs is blunt about which road prospers. Concealing does not just cost you integrity; it costs you mercy — because mercy only reaches the things we bring into the light. This is the strange arithmetic of the gospel: the one who admits the failure is the one who walks out free. Christ did not die to protect your track record; he died so your track record could stop being the point. When a founder says “I was wrong” out loud, something shifts in a company. The team learns that honesty is survivable here. Bad news starts traveling faster than spin. And you discover that the authority you feared losing was never held up by your infallibility — it was held up by trust, and trust grows best in confessed soil. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you know the call I got wrong and the ways I have been polishing the story since. I do not want to manage this; I want to confess it. Thank you that in Christ my standing does not depend on a spotless record. Give me the courage to say plainly to my team what I am saying now to you. <break time="1.1s" /> I will name my mistake to the people it affected, in plain words, without a single excuse attached. <break time="1.1s" /> Walk out of hiding today, and let mercy do what image management never could. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-hu-selfmade: On the Self-Made Myth. <break time="1.8s" /> Come and count what you have been given. Even your ability to build was on loan before you ever used it. <break time="1.1s" /> “For who makes you different from anyone else? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” <break time="1.1s" />1 Corinthians 4, verse 7. <break time="1.1s" /> “Self-made” is the most flattering lie in the founder vocabulary. Yes, you worked — brutally, probably. But Paul’s question cuts underneath the work: “What do you have that you did not receive?” Trace anything you are proud of far enough back and you find a gift. The mind that solves problems: given. The parents, the mentor who took your call, the market timing, the country you launched in, the body that survived the hard year: given, given, given. Self-sufficiency feels like a virtue — no handouts, no favors, nobody’s help. But hiding inside it is the oldest pride there is: the refusal to be a receiver. And that pride costs more than accuracy. It cuts you off from gratitude, from asking for help, and finally from grace itself — because grace, by definition, can only be received. The gospel meets the self-made founder with a gentler accounting: everything is a gift, including the rescue you could not engineer. Those who know this hold their companies loosely and their thanksgiving tightly. They built something real. They just know who provided the materials. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, forgive me for taking credit for the materials. I did the work, but you gave the mind, the moment, the people, and the strength — and I have called the sum of your gifts my achievement. Teach me to receive: help, counsel, grace, all of it. Make me a grateful builder instead of a self-made one. <break time="1.1s" /> I will write down five things behind my company’s success that I did nothing to earn, and thank God for each one. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and build with open hands, remembering the Giver in everything you are tempted to call your own. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-hu-praise: On Being Tested by Praise. <break time="1.8s" /> Come, before the applause fades, and stand where a louder voice can reach you. The crucible is already warm. <break time="1.1s" /> “The crucible for silver and the furnace for gold, but people are tested by their praise.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 27, verse 21. <break time="1.1s" /> Proverbs says people are tested by their praise, and every founder who has had a good press cycle knows the exam. The crucible does not destroy silver; it reveals what it is made of. Praise works the same way. The article runs, the round closes, the follower count jumps — and something in you begins, quietly, to believe the copy. Criticism rarely ruins a founder; flattery does it slower and more pleasantly. The test is not whether praise comes but what it finds when it arrives. Does it land on an identity already settled — beloved of God, secure before the coverage and after it — or does it land on a hunger that will now need feeding? Jesus heard crowds shout “Hosanna” and did not adjust his course by a degree, because his Father’s voice was louder than theirs. That is the aim: not to refuse encouragement, which is churlish, but to metabolize it as gratitude instead of fuel. Enjoy the good week. Send the article to your mom. Then get up tomorrow as the same servant you were before anyone was watching. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, thank you for the encouragement of this season — I receive it as kindness from your hand. But keep my ear tuned to your voice above the crowd’s, because crowds turn and you do not. Let praise pass through me as gratitude rather than settle in me as need. Keep me the same person in public that I am before you in secret. <break time="1.1s" /> I will pass on the credit today, naming specifically the people and the God who made the good news possible. <break time="1.1s" /> Carry the applause lightly, and let your Father’s voice remain the loudest one you hear. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-hu-freedom: On Not Being the Smartest. <break time="1.8s" /> Come and set down the exhausting act of knowing everything. There is a lower place, and it is restful there. <break time="1.1s" /> “Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, that he may lift you up in due time. Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you.” <break time="1.1s" />1 Peter 5, verses 6 to 7. <break time="1.1s" /> Notice what Peter puts next to humility: anxiety. “Humble yourselves… cast all your anxiety on him.” The two sentences are one thought, because the pride that makes you pose as the smartest person in the room is the same pride that keeps you up at night. If everything depends on your brain, then every gap in your knowledge is a threat, every brilliant hire a rival, every question you cannot answer a small exposure. That is an exhausting way to live, and it quietly caps your company at the size of your own head. Humility is the exit. Under God’s mighty hand there is nothing left to prove — he already knows exactly how smart you are, and loves you anyway, and the lifting up is his job, not yours. So you are free to say the three most liberating sentences in leadership: “I don’t know.” “What do you think?” “You’re right.” The room fills with better thinking the moment you stop needing to supply all of it. That is not a loss of stature. It is rest. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, I am tired of performing omniscience. I humble myself under your mighty hand and hand you the anxiety that came bundled with my pride. Thank you that you know my limits fully and love me anyway. Free me to ask, to listen, and to be gladly outthought by the people you have given me. <break time="1.1s" /> I will say “I don’t know — what do you think?” in my next meeting instead of improvising an answer. <break time="1.1s" /> Go in the freedom of the lifted burden, and let God be the one who raises you up. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-fo-replay: On the Argument You Keep Replaying. <break time="1.8s" /> There is a conversation you have had a hundred times, and the other person was only present for the first one. Sit still and notice how much of you it is renting. <break time="1.1s" /> “Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you.” <break time="1.1s" />Colossians 3, verse 13. <break time="1.1s" /> You win the replay every time. In the shower, on the drive, in the quiet before sleep, you say the thing you should have said, and the partner or investor or client finally sees how wrong they were. But no one is convinced by these victories, and no one pays for them except you. Paul does not pretend grievances are rare — “if any of you has a grievance” assumes you will. What he interrupts is the loop. Forgive as the Lord forgave you: not after you had explained yourself, not once the accounts were settled, but while the wrong was still warm. The replay is your heart trying to get justice by rehearsal, and rehearsal cannot deliver it. Forgiveness is not deciding the argument didn’t matter. It is handing the file to Someone with better judgment than your shower speeches, and walking out of the room where the fight lives. You may have to hand it over again tomorrow. Grace is patient with people who forgive in installments. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Lord, you know the argument I keep winning in my head and losing in my heart. I hand you the grievance, the unsaid speech, the verdict I keep demanding. Forgive them through me, the way you forgave me before I ever apologized. Quiet the replay and give the room back to peace. <break time="1.1s" /> I will notice the replay when it starts today, and hand the argument to God instead of finishing it. <break time="1.1s" /> Go and leave the courtroom in your head unattended — the Judge you trust is already seated. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.8s" />Amen.<break time="1.1s" />
d-fo-boundaries: On Forgiving With Your Eyes Open. <break time="1.8s" /> Somewhere you learned that real forgiveness means acting like it never happened. Set that down before you begin — it isn’t in the Book. <break time="1.1s" /> “Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.” <break time="1.1s" />Proverbs 4, verse 23. <break time="1.1s" /> Forgiveness cancels a debt; it does not shred the lesson. You can release someone from what they owe you and still decline to hand them the keys again. The same Bible that commands mercy also commands this: above all else, guard your heart. Those are not rival instructions. Wisdom and mercy can share an office. When you forgive the vendor who cut corners, the co-founder who went behind your back, the client who never paid, you are letting go of the right to make them hurt for it. You are not swearing that the past is inadmissible. Pretending it didn’t happen is not grace; it is amnesia, and amnesia is a poor steward of the people and payroll God has put in your care. So write the tighter contract. Add the second signature. Keep the boundary — and keep it without contempt, the way a good fence stands without shouting. The test of your forgiveness is not whether you trust them again tomorrow. It is whether you can pray for their good today and mean it. <break time="1.1s" /> <break time="1.1s" />Let’s pray.<break time="1.8s" /> Father, teach me the difference between a grudge and a guardrail.
